guide.title: Metformin
guide.description: How metformin works, its investigated benefits across infections, cancer, neurological conditions and physical function, and its safety.

sections.label: Overview
sections.title: What is metformin?
sections.paragraph: Metformin is an oral glucose-lowering medicine in the biguanide class. In the United States, immediate-release metformin tablets are approved alongside diet and exercise for type 2 diabetes in adults and children aged 10 years and older. It reduces the liver’s glucose production and improves the body’s response to insulin; those established uses are distinct from the repurposing investigations discussed here. Researchers are studying whether its effects on metabolism, cellular energy sensing and inflammatory pathways can help in acute COVID-19 and Long COVID, Parkinson’s disease, cognition in schizophrenia, and age-related loss of muscle function. Cancer research includes trials in prostate, lung, breast and pancreatic cancer, studies of recurrent colorectal adenomas after polyp removal, and laboratory work in multiple myeloma. The findings vary by condition and outcome: promising biological effects have often failed to translate into clinical benefit, and preventing a condition, treating established disease and changing a laboratory marker are different questions.

sections.label: Benefits
sections.paragraph: The benefits being investigated include reducing Long COVID risk, improving cognition in schizophrenia, preserving physical function in older adults and improving Parkinson’s symptoms. A small schizophrenia trial reported improved cognitive-test scores with metformin, while the Parkinson’s pilot and the MET-PREVENT sarcopenia trial did not demonstrate improvements in their main clinical outcomes. For Long COVID, COVID-OUT reported a prevention signal, although a correction notice and inconsistent control percentages complicate interpretation; ACTIV-6 did not meet its primary efficacy threshold, and a separate trial found no improved recovery after symptoms were established. Cancer trials have generally not demonstrated the hoped-for treatment benefits; a separate colorectal study found fewer recurrent adenomas after polyp removal, which is a prevention outcome.

questions.question: Does metformin improve symptoms of Parkinson’s disease?
questions.answer: A three-month pilot randomized 60 people to metformin or placebo alongside levodopa/carbidopa. Clinical scores improved within the metformin group, but the comparison between groups did not show a statistically significant benefit on the total Unified Parkinson’s Disease Rating Scale. The trial was small, used a per-protocol analysis and was too short to establish whether metformin slows disease progression.

questions.question: What has the schizophrenia research found about cognition?
questions.answer: In a 72-person open-label randomized trial, adding metformin to antipsychotic treatment improved the composite cognitive-test score by an estimated 3.43 points more than antipsychotics alone after 24 weeks (95% CI 1.83–5.02). The participants were predominantly young adults, 59 completed follow-up, and the study lacked a placebo group; larger blinded studies are needed to confirm the size and practical importance of this effect. A later analysis of the same trial linked changes in metabolites and hippocampal connectivity with cognitive changes.

questions.question: Does metformin improve muscle strength or physical function?
questions.answer: The 2025 MET-PREVENT trial randomized 72 older adults with probable sarcopenia and prefrailty or frailty to metformin or placebo for four months. It found no walking-speed benefit: the adjusted difference was 0.001 m/s (95% CI −0.06 to 0.06), and metformin was poorly tolerated in this population. The 2023 review described inconsistent results: some research suggested faster walking, but strength outcomes were not consistently improved and exercise adaptations could be reduced. In the MASTERS trial, adding metformin to resistance training reduced muscle growth in healthy older adults; the difference in strength gains was not statistically significant.

questions.question: Does taking metformin during COVID-19 prevent Long COVID?
questions.answer: COVID-OUT reported fewer later clinician-diagnosed cases when treatment began during acute infection, but the estimate remains provisional because the report contains inconsistent control percentages and has a published correction. ACTIV-6 examined symptoms attributed to COVID-19 or death at six months and did not meet its prespecified threshold for benefit. The trials enrolled different populations and used different outcomes, leaving uncertainty about how much prevention benefit metformin provides.

questions.question: Does metformin help when Long COVID is already established?
questions.answer: A randomized South Korean trial did not find improved recovery after a two-week course of metformin in people with persistent symptoms. That result concerns the population and short treatment course tested; it does not establish the effect of longer courses or treatment in every Long COVID subgroup. A separate metformin-and-fluvoxamine fatigue report was retracted and republished; its original findings cannot serve as reliable evidence of metformin benefit.

questions.answer: COVID-OUT did not meet its primary composite endpoint combining hypoxemia, emergency-department attendance, hospitalization or death. That acute endpoint is separate from later Long COVID diagnosis.

questions.question: Does metformin improve prostate-cancer survival?
questions.answer: STAMPEDE randomized 1,874 men with metastatic hormone-sensitive disease. Overall survival did not improve significantly: hazard ratio 0.91, 95% CI 0.80–1.03. Adverse metabolic effects of androgen deprivation were reduced.

questions.question: Does adding metformin help in lung cancer?
questions.answer: NRG-LU001 found no survival improvement with metformin added to chemoradiation. OCOG-ALMERA also found no benefit and reported worse survival estimates in the metformin group.

questions.question: Is the colorectal finding about cancer treatment or prevention?
questions.answer: It concerns prevention of recurrent adenomas and polyps after removal. In the one-year trial, adenoma recurrence was lower with 250 mg daily metformin, with a reported risk ratio of 0.60, 95% CI 0.39–0.92. Survival after established cancer was not the endpoint.

questions.answer: Adding metformin to gemcitabine and erlotinib did not improve survival in a 121-person trial: overall-survival hazard ratio 1.056, 95% CI 0.72–1.55.

questions.answer: The cited experiment found slower myeloma-cell and xenograft growth. It tested cell cultures and mice, so it provides an experimental finding rather than a measured patient benefit.

sections.label: Safety
sections.paragraph: Metformin commonly causes diarrhea, nausea, vomiting, gas and abdominal discomfort, while prolonged treatment can lower vitamin B12 concentrations. Its boxed warning concerns lactic acidosis, a potentially fatal buildup of acid associated with metformin accumulation. Kidney impairment is particularly important because the drug is eliminated through the kidneys; hypoxic illness, liver impairment, excessive alcohol use and certain interacting medicines add risk. The label also identifies surgery, restricted food or fluid intake and some iodinated-contrast procedures as situations requiring a separate interruption and kidney-function assessment. Metformin alone does not normally stimulate insulin release, but hypoglycemia becomes more likely when it is combined with insulin or an insulin secretagogue. Periodic kidney assessment, blood counts and vitamin B12 assessment address different hazards. These precautions concern the labeled oral product and remain relevant when research proposes using the same medicine outside diabetes.

sections.label: Contraindications
sections.paragraph: The tablet label lists three formal contraindications: severe kidney impairment, hypersensitivity to metformin, and acute or chronic metabolic acidosis, including diabetic ketoacidosis. Severe kidney impairment is defined as an estimated glomerular filtration rate below 30 mL/min/1.73 m². A different threshold governs starting treatment: initiation is not recommended when this estimate is between 30 and 45. If kidney function subsequently falls below 45 during established treatment, the label calls for reassessing the balance of benefit and risk, rather than treating that threshold as identical to the absolute contraindication below 30. Iodinated contrast, hypoxic illness, excessive alcohol consumption and liver impairment introduce additional precautions and interruption decisions. Those situations must remain distinct from the formal contraindication list. The restrictions also concern the actual patient and formulation; eligibility for one repurposing trial does not establish that every other patient can safely receive metformin.

sections.label: Interactions
sections.paragraph: Metformin interactions can increase drug exposure, worsen susceptibility to acidosis, or increase hypoglycemia when another glucose-lowering medicine is present. Drugs that reduce renal clearance, including cimetidine, dolutegravir and ranolazine, can increase metformin accumulation. Carbonic anhydrase inhibitors such as topiramate can lower bicarbonate and contribute to metabolic acidosis, creating a different interaction pathway. Excessive alcohol intake affects lactate metabolism and is another concern in the lactic-acidosis warning. Insulin and sulfonylureas can increase hypoglycemia risk even though metformin itself does not stimulate insulin secretion. Other medicines can raise blood glucose and affect diabetes control, so stopping or starting them can also change the clinical context. These categories are not interchangeable: an exposure interaction is different from additive glucose lowering or an acid-base effect. The label describes them alongside kidney-function and acute-illness precautions, rather than providing a blanket clearance for any proposed repurposing combination.

sections.label: Dosing
sections.title: What schedules have repurposing trials tested?
sections.paragraph: The COVID-OUT and ACTIV-6 prevention trials tested a 14-day course of immediate-release metformin, increasing to 1,500 mg daily. The Parkinson’s pilot used 500 mg twice daily for three months, while the schizophrenia trial used up to 1,500 mg daily for 24 weeks. These studies tested different treatment schedules for different conditions; they did not establish one repurposing dose or demonstrate equivalent outcomes with extended-release metformin. The immediate-release tablet label describes administration with meals and gradual increases according to tolerability and glucose control, rather than one starting schedule for every patient. Its adult maximum is different from its pediatric maximum, and kidney-function restrictions apply before treatment and during follow-up. Those labeled diabetes schedules must be kept separate from the short prevention courses and longer research regimens summarized above.

questions.question: What are the labeled starting dose and titration schedule for immediate-release metformin?
questions.answer: The U.S. prescribing information for immediate-release metformin tablets lists a starting dose of 500 mg twice daily or 850 mg once daily, taken with meals. The dose is increased by 500 mg each week or by 850 mg every two weeks, based on glycemic control and tolerability, up to a maximum of 2,550 mg per day in divided doses. The label notes that doses above 2,000 mg per day may be better tolerated when divided into three doses taken with meals. These are the labeled regimens for type 2 diabetes; repurposing trials used their own schedules.

questions.question: What is the labeled starting dose and maximum for extended-release metformin?
questions.answer: The U.S. prescribing information for extended-release metformin tablets recommends starting at 500 mg once daily with the evening meal. The dose is increased by 500 mg each week based on glycemic control and tolerability, up to a maximum of 2,000 mg once daily with the evening meal. The label states that patients already receiving immediate-release metformin may switch to the same total daily dose as extended-release taken once daily. The extended-release label does not include a pediatric dosing section.

questions.question: Do immediate-release and extended-release metformin have the same efficacy and tolerability?
questions.answer: A 2021 systematic review and meta-analysis of nine randomized controlled trials in 2,609 adults with type 2 diabetes found that extended-release metformin produced statistically worse but likely clinically similar HbA1c lowering compared with immediate-release. Extended-release reduced dyspepsia relative to immediate-release but did not significantly reduce overall gastrointestinal intolerance, including diarrhea, abdominal discomfort, and nausea. The U.S. prescribing information for each formulation describes its own dosing regimen and does not assert equivalent glycemic efficacy across formulations.

questions.question: How should metformin dosing be adjusted based on kidney function?
questions.answer: Both the immediate-release and extended-release U.S. prescribing information require assessment of kidney function (eGFR) before starting metformin and periodically during treatment. Starting metformin is not recommended when eGFR is 30 to 45 mL/min/1.73 m2; metformin is contraindicated and should be discontinued when eGFR falls below 30 mL/min/1.73 m2. A 2014 systematic review in JAMA of metformin in type 2 diabetes and kidney disease found that lactate concentrations are not substantially increased at eGFR values of 30 to 60 mL/min/1.73 m2, and concluded that cautious use with dose monitoring is warranted in mild-to-moderate chronic kidney disease.

sections.label: Quality
sections.paragraph: Metformin product identity includes its release formulation, tablet strength and intended dosing schedule. The immediate-release and extended-release labels describe different administration patterns; an extended-release tablet is designed to release its contents over time and is swallowed whole, rather than crushed or chewed. An immediate-release regimen used in a trial therefore cannot be converted into an extended-release research regimen simply by matching the total milligrams. The two products also have their own dose-increase instructions and labeled limits. FDA-approved generic products must meet the relevant requirements for the reference product, including active ingredient, strength, dosage form, route and bioequivalence. That regulatory comparison concerns a specified reference formulation. It does not establish that every release formulation, compounded preparation or differently scheduled product reproduces the exposure or clinical findings of a particular repurposing trial.

sections.label: Evidence
sections.paragraph: The human evidence spans prevention, treatment and physical or cognitive function, with different populations, comparators and follow-up periods. Several cancer trials did not demonstrate the expected clinical benefit; adenoma recurrence after polyp removal is a separate prevention outcome. The schizophrenia metabolite and imaging report analyzes the same trial as the earlier cognitive report, so it does not add a second independent trial. Cell and mouse findings explain biological rationale but cannot establish patient benefit. COVID-OUT has a published correction notice and conflicting control-group percentages in the available report. Its long-term diagnosis estimate should be read with that qualification. The original REVIVE fatigue report has a notice of retraction and republication; its original results are not used as evidence of benefit.

guide.title: Fluvoxamine
guide.description: An OCD medicine investigated for inflammatory effects in acute COVID-19 and persistent fatigue.

sections.label: Overview
sections.paragraph: Fluvoxamine is an SSRI used for OCD. In acute COVID-19, a later randomized trial did not show faster sustained recovery. Its established action blocks serotonin reuptake, increasing serotonin signaling, while the repurposing rationale concerns inflammatory signaling rather than an extension of the OCD indication. ACTIV-6 tested treatment during an acute infection and defined sustained recovery as three consecutive days without symptoms. Median recovery was 10 days in both groups. That result does not establish a treatment effect in people who already have Long COVID. The separate original REVIVE fatigue report carries a retraction-and-republication notice, so its original estimate cannot be used to claim relief of persistent fatigue. Established psychiatric use, an experimental anti-inflammatory rationale and a measured COVID-19 outcome therefore remain distinct parts of the evidence.

sections.paragraph: Nausea, sleep disturbance and sexual dysfunction are recognized adverse effects; serious risks include serotonin syndrome, bleeding and increased suicidal thinking in younger patients. Serious adverse events were uncommon in ACTIV-6, so the trial offers limited precision about rare harms. The absence of an observed excess in that selected outpatient sample does not establish that fluvoxamine is suitable for everyone. The study excluded several groups, including people using certain antidepressants and those with known contraindications; trial tolerability does not remove the separate prescribing restrictions. Both groups had a median recovery time of 10 days, with no demonstrated acceleration from fluvoxamine. It also does not describe treatment of established Long COVID. guide.description: An antiviral combination used early in high-risk COVID-19 and tested separately for established Long COVID.

sections.label: Overview
sections.paragraph: Paxlovid is indicated for mild to moderate COVID-19 in adults at high risk of severe disease. Trials of longer courses for established Long COVID have not demonstrated the expected symptom advantage. The co-packaged tablets have separate roles: nirmatrelvir interrupts viral protein processing and ritonavir slows nirmatrelvir breakdown. That antiviral action underlies the acute-infection indication, which is restricted to adults at high risk of progression. Research in established Long COVID asks a different question about symptoms continuing after the initial illness. STOP-PASC tested 15 days rather than the labeled five-day acute course. Both STOP-PASC and RECOVER-VITAL reported no significant primary symptom advantage in their studied Long COVID populations. The approved acute use therefore does not establish effectiveness for persistent symptoms or validate extending treatment for that purpose.

For acute infection, the prescribing information specifies adults at high risk of progression to hospitalization or death. The persistent-symptom trials should be read separately from that approved role. STOP-PASC did not find significant pooled symptom improvement after its 15-day course. RECOVER-VITAL also reported no significant primary benefit in the cognitive, autonomic and exercise-intolerance groups it studied. They do show that the rationale for extending antiviral exposure did not produce the expected primary clinical advantage in those comparisons.

sections.label: Safety
sections.paragraph: Nirmatrelvir with ritonavir has a safety profile dominated by ritonavir's strong inhibition of CYP3A, an enzyme involved in clearing many medicines. An interacting drug can accumulate enough to cause severe, life-threatening or fatal effects, so the label's boxed warning makes medication review central to treatment. Common reported reactions include altered taste and diarrhea, but these are distinct from serious hypersensitivity reactions and the hepatic risks associated with ritonavir. Kidney impairment also changes the appropriate dose pack and schedule because nirmatrelvir exposure rises when renal clearance is reduced. Severe liver impairment is a separate setting in which the product is not recommended. The labeled treatment is a short course for eligible adults with acute COVID-19; that defined exposure does not establish the safety or effectiveness of prolonged courses, different combinations or treatment of established Long COVID.

sections.label: Contraindications
sections.paragraph: The product is contraindicated after a clinically significant hypersensitivity reaction to nirmatrelvir, ritonavir or another component. Its other major contraindications concern specified interacting medicines. One group consists of drugs primarily metabolized by CYP3A for which increased concentrations can cause serious or life-threatening reactions. Another consists of potent CYP3A inducers that can reduce antiviral concentrations enough to compromise the response and permit resistance. Stopping an inducer immediately before antiviral treatment may not remove its effect because enzyme induction can persist. These restrictions are different from dose adjustment for kidney impairment and from the recommendation against use in severe liver impairment. The actual interacting medicine, its clearance pathway and the consequences of changing its exposure determine the restriction. A general statement that a patient takes several medicines cannot replace the product-specific interaction assessment required by the label.

sections.paragraph: Ritonavir is included to inhibit metabolism and sustain nirmatrelvir exposure, but that same pharmacology changes the exposure of many other medicines. The label distinguishes combinations that are contraindicated from those requiring interruption, dose adjustment or additional monitoring. Clinically important examples span antiarrhythmics, anticoagulants, anticonvulsants, lipid-lowering medicines and immunosuppressants, with different instructions for individual agents. Strong enzyme inducers create the opposite problem by lowering antiviral concentrations, and their effects may persist after withdrawal. This is why a recently stopped drug can still matter. Kidney function, the competing medicine's therapeutic range and the feasibility of changing its regimen all affect interpretation. These interactions cannot be summarized as a single drug-class prohibition or assumed absent because the antiviral course lasts only five days. The source is the co-packaged nirmatrelvir/ritonavir product label, not a study of unrestricted repurposing combinations.

sections.paragraph: The marketed product contains separate nirmatrelvir and ritonavir tablets packaged together, rather than one tablet containing both active ingredients. Nirmatrelvir supplies the antiviral action, while ritonavir changes its exposure through metabolic inhibition. The packaging therefore helps identify both components and their scheduled administration. Tablet identity, tablet count and the actual renal regimen matter alongside the product name. These product-specific distinctions also limit interpretation of repurposing research: a study of the combination does not test nirmatrelvir alone, ritonavir alone, an arbitrary mixture of antiviral medicines or a longer unstudied course. Matching the printed strength of one component would not reproduce the complete labeled exposure and schedule.

guide.title: Naltrexone
guide.description: An opioid receptor blocker investigated at lower doses for fatigue and pain, and at conventional doses for compulsive sexual behavior.

sections.label: Overview
sections.paragraph: Naltrexone has established addiction-treatment uses. Repurposing evidence differs by condition: an uncontrolled Long COVID cohort reported improvements, while a larger fibromyalgia trial did not show a significant pain benefit. Its established action is competitive blockade of opioid receptors, and the oral tablet label covers alcohol dependence and blockade of exogenous opioids. Repurposing studies do not all test the same dose or outcome. The Long COVID cohort followed 59 patients without a randomized comparison. The fibromyalgia trial tested 6 mg daily, while the compulsive-behavior trial used 50 mg daily. A separate ME/CFS experiment measured a calcium-permeable channel in isolated immune cells. Those distinctions matter because patient symptom changes, a randomized pain comparison and a laboratory channel result provide different kinds of information about the investigated uses.

Fibromyalgia pain did not improve significantly more than with placebo in the 99-woman trial; compulsive-behavior findings varied by the outcome measure. The 59-patient Long COVID report associated treatment with fewer symptoms and improved functional status, but provides no placebo-adjusted response estimate. In fibromyalgia, the 12-week between-group pain difference was -0.34 points, with a confidence interval from -0.95 to 0.27, so a significant pain advantage was not demonstrated. In the 73-man compulsive sexual behavior trial, clinical interviews favored active treatment while self-report questionnaires did not separate it from placebo. That trial did not study persistent genital arousal disorder or genitopelvic dysesthesia. Its behavioral findings therefore cannot establish relief of persistent unwanted genital sensations in those different conditions.

sections.label: Safety
sections.paragraph: Naltrexone can cause nausea, headache, dizziness, fatigue and other adverse reactions, but its opioid-antagonist action creates several distinctive serious hazards. Starting it while a person remains dependent on opioids can precipitate abrupt withdrawal severe enough to require hospital or intensive care. Attempting to overcome its receptor blockade with large opioid doses can cause fatal overdose. After treatment stops and the blockade wanes, reduced opioid tolerance can also make previously tolerated amounts dangerous. The tablet label separately describes hepatitis and clinically significant liver dysfunction, as well as reports of depression or suicidal thinking that require attention to the clinical context. Low-dose repurposing schedules do not establish that these pharmacological concerns disappear. Opioid exposure, the actual dose and formulation, liver status and the availability of an appropriate pain-management plan all remain relevant to interpreting an individual study's safety findings.

sections.label: Contraindications
sections.paragraph: The oral naltrexone label contraindicates treatment in patients receiving opioid analgesics, those currently dependent on opioids, and those in acute opioid withdrawal. Dependence includes maintenance treatment with an opioid agonist such as methadone or a partial agonist such as buprenorphine. A positive opioid urine screen or a failed naloxone challenge is another stated contraindication, and sensitivity to naltrexone or a product component is listed separately. These restrictions follow from receptor blockade and the possibility of severe precipitated withdrawal. The label also explains that a negative screen or challenge does not completely exclude that possibility, particularly during transitions from certain maintenance treatments. A low-dose research regimen is therefore not a general exception to opioid-related assessment. Formal contraindications, liver-related warnings and the trial's own eligibility criteria describe different boundaries and should not be merged into one undifferentiated exclusion list.

sections.label: Interactions
sections.paragraph: Naltrexone can block the effects of opioid-containing medicines, including some analgesics, cough preparations and antidiarrheal products. This is a pharmacodynamic interaction at opioid receptors, rather than simply competition for the same metabolic enzyme. The label describes special difficulties when emergency opioid analgesia is required: larger opioid amounts may be needed, but respiratory depression can then be deeper and more prolonged. It also warns that attempts to overcome the blockade outside an appropriate medical setting can be fatal. Evidence for interactions with non-opioid drugs is less complete; the tablet label states that dedicated studies of many such combinations have not been performed. It specifically discusses the uncertain safety of concurrent disulfiram and reports of lethargy or somnolence with thioridazine. These limits mean that absence of a listed interaction is not a completed assessment of an arbitrary repurposing combination.

guide.title: Pramipexole
guide.description: A dopamine agonist with randomized evidence as an add-on for treatment-resistant unipolar depression.

sections.label: Overview
sections.paragraph: Pramipexole is a dopamine agonist used for Parkinson’s disease and restless legs syndrome. PAX-D found improvement when it was added for treatment-resistant unipolar depression. Label context: Pramipexole stimulates the D2 family of dopamine receptors, with greater affinity for D3. The precise mechanisms of its Parkinson and restless-legs benefits remain incompletely understood; receptor binding alone does not establish an antidepressant effect. Clinical evidence: Low for the currently usable PAX-D result. The randomized trial reported greater improvement in depressive symptoms with pramipexole augmentation than placebo at twelve weeks. The existing assessment remains provisional because an indexed correction has not been reconciled. Adverse-event discontinuations were higher with pramipexole, and the trial does not establish superiority to another active augmentation treatment.

sections.label: Safety
sections.paragraph: Pramipexole can cause nausea, sleepiness, dizziness and orthostatic hypotension, but its warnings extend beyond those common symptoms. Patients have reported suddenly falling asleep during ordinary activities, sometimes without an obvious warning of drowsiness. Hallucinations, psychotic-like behavior and impulse-control problems, including compulsive gambling, spending or sexual behavior, are additional concerns with dopamine-agonist treatment. Kidney impairment increases exposure because renal elimination is important, while the indication and dose schedule affect tolerability. The label also describes withdrawal-related symptoms and the need to distinguish discontinuation effects from the underlying disorder. These issues are relevant to depression research as well as the established movement-disorder uses: a change in the treatment goal does not change the medicine's receptor activity. Trial safety findings must therefore retain their actual dose, population, co-medications and follow-up rather than becoming a general claim that psychiatric or repurposed use is well tolerated.

sections.paragraph: The cited pramipexole tablet label lists no formal contraindications. That statement must remain separate from its substantial warnings and dose restrictions. The label describes sudden sleep episodes, symptomatic orthostatic hypotension, hallucinations and psychotic-like behavior, and urges assessment of impulse-control or compulsive behaviors. Reduced kidney function can require a different dose or titration schedule because the drug is predominantly cleared through the kidneys. Co-administered sedatives and other dopamine-active medicines also affect the clinical context. These are not converted into formal contraindications simply because they are consequential, and absence of a formal contraindication is not proof that a particular person or investigational indication has been assessed. The distinction is especially important when reading treatment-resistant-depression studies: their screening rules and exclusions characterize the people studied, while the product label describes a different set of pharmacological precautions.

Cimetidine inhibits renal tubular secretion and increases pramipexole exposure; other medicines using the same renal transport pathway may also matter. Dopamine antagonists can oppose the intended receptor action, making the pharmacological relationship different from an interaction that raises blood concentrations. Alcohol and sedating medicines are relevant to the warning about sleepiness and sudden sleep episodes. In Parkinson's disease, co-treatment with levodopa can also affect adverse effects such as dyskinesia and the required clinical adjustments. These mechanisms should be considered separately instead of assigning all combinations the same risk or severity. The cited label supports interpretation of the oral tablet, while a psychiatric repurposing trial tests only its stated regimen and co-medications. An untested drug combination cannot be cleared by assuming that pramipexole has little hepatic metabolism.

guide.title: Long COVID
guide.description: What Long COVID is, why existing medicines are being studied, and what the prevention and treatment trials found.

sections.label: Overview
sections.paragraph: Long COVID can involve persistent or recurring fatigue, problems with thinking, breathlessness and worsening symptoms after physical or mental effort. Symptoms can affect several body systems and continue for months or years. Repurposing studies ask two different questions: whether treatment during acute infection reduces later illness, and whether treatment helps people who already have persistent symptoms. The distinction between prevention and treatment is central to interpreting these studies. A drug started during an acute infection is being tested before the later condition is established; a course given to someone with ongoing symptoms addresses a different clinical problem. Post-exertional worsening can follow physical or mental activity and should be assessed directly when it is a treatment target. A change in a diagnosis rate therefore does not by itself demonstrate recovery of thinking, breathing or activity tolerance among people already living with Long COVID.

In established illness, the South Korean trial did not find improved recovery after its tested metformin course. STOP-PASC and RECOVER-VITAL evaluated nirmatrelvir-ritonavir in selected symptom groups and did not show their expected primary benefits. These are separate intervention questions: an unsuccessful treatment trial does not directly refute prevention, while a prevention signal does not establish relief of persistent symptoms. sections.paragraph: These trials did not directly compare metformin with nirmatrelvir-ritonavir for the same population and outcome. Prevention during infection, recovery after established illness and improvement in particular symptoms are separate comparisons. For example, COVID-OUT asked whether acute-phase metformin changed later Long COVID diagnoses, whereas the South Korean metformin trial asked about recovery in established illness. STOP-PASC studied nirmatrelvir-ritonavir in people who already had persistent symptoms. The same word, improvement, can therefore refer to avoiding a diagnosis, recovering from illness or changing a symptom score. These endpoints cannot be ranked as though the drugs had competed in a single head-to-head trial. Treatment timing and the population studied must accompany any numerical comparison, and a result for one endpoint cannot supply an unmeasured effect on fatigue, cognition or post-exertional worsening.

guide.title: Acute COVID-19
guide.description: Repurposed medicines in acute COVID-19: antiviral treatment, inflammatory pathways and randomized results.

sections.label: Overview
sections.paragraph: Acute COVID-19 is the illness caused by a current SARS-CoV-2 infection. Its course ranges from mild respiratory symptoms to severe illness, with older age and certain medical conditions increasing risk. Drug studies have tested ways to reduce viral replication or the harmful host response before illness progresses. The treatment question depends on the phase and severity of illness. Early outpatient antiviral treatment targets viral replication within a short period after symptom onset, whereas a hospitalized-patient study addresses a different clinical setting. COVID-OUT examined metformin, ivermectin and fluvoxamine in nonhospitalized adults with overweight or obesity. RECOVERY tested hydroxychloroquine in hospitalized patients. Neither the population nor the endpoint can be assumed to transfer between those settings. Research on progression during the infection is also distinct from later follow-up for Long COVID: preventing an acute event, shortening symptoms and reducing a future diagnosis are separate clinical goals.

sections.paragraph: The COVID-OUT trial tested metformin, ivermectin and fluvoxamine in adults with overweight or obesity. None significantly reduced its primary composite of hypoxemia, emergency care, hospitalization or death. Nirmatrelvir with ritonavir has a separate established role in early treatment of eligible people at higher risk of severe COVID-19. Other cited studies address different repurposing questions. PRINCIPLE found no clinically meaningful recovery or hospitalization benefit from doxycycline in older or vulnerable community patients. The higher-dose ACTIV-6 fluvoxamine trial did not accelerate sustained symptom recovery. RECOVERY found no reduction in 28-day mortality from hydroxychloroquine in hospitalized patients. These findings do not all measure the same outcome, and they should not be combined into a single drug ranking. In particular, the later COVID-OUT Long COVID follow-up asks about subsequent illness rather than the acute composite outcome; a result from that follow-up cannot replace the primary acute-treatment finding.

sections.label: Safety
sections.paragraph: Ritonavir creates important drug-interaction constraints, and kidney and liver function affect treatment selection. Early antiviral treatment also has a short window from symptom onset. An early-treatment recommendation therefore includes both eligibility and the ability to use the medicine safely with a person's existing regimen. The ritonavir component is especially relevant when reviewing other prescriptions, rather than treating a positive SARS-CoV-2 test as sufficient reason to use the combination. Kidney and liver function are separate considerations that affect treatment selection within the short treatment window. The cited outpatient guidance addresses eligible people at higher risk of progression, so the suitability assessment belongs to that population and timing. These restrictions also mean that a result for one drug or a selected trial group cannot establish safety for every antiviral, every coadministered medicine or treatment begun later in the illness.

sections.paragraph: Hospitalization prevention in a high-risk group cannot be equated with shortening mild symptoms in a lower-risk group. Its composite also combines oxygen measurements with health-care use and death, so a composite result is not a precise mortality estimate. PRINCIPLE's doxycycline comparison concerns recovery and hospitalization in older or vulnerable community patients, while RECOVERY's hydroxychloroquine comparison concerns hospitalized illness and 28-day mortality. Keeping these distinctions visible prevents a result for recovery in one setting from being presented as proof of hospitalization prevention in another, or an acute result from being substituted for a Long COVID outcome.

sections.label: Evidence
sections.paragraph: COVID-OUT was placebo-controlled and enrolled nonhospitalized adults with overweight or obesity. Its primary outcome combined oxygen saturation, emergency care, hospitalization and death; component and later follow-up results answer narrower questions. The fluvoxamine and ivermectin comparisons belong to the same factorial trial family, with different concurrent-control groups; their participant counts must not be added as independent trials. Home oximetry contributed much of the primary composite and had measurement and reporting limitations. Consequently, absence of a significant composite reduction does not supply a precise separate estimate for death alone. The later Long COVID report uses another follow-up period and a diagnosis endpoint, while ACTIV-6 used three consecutive symptom-free days for recovery. These design choices determine what each result can answer. A source-specific conclusion retains the drug, eligible population, timing, outcome definition and uncertainty rather than combining incompatible measures.

guide.title: Epithelial ovarian or fallopian-tube carcinoma
guide.description: Epithelial ovarian and fallopian-tube cancers, and the evidence behind itraconazole combinations.

sections.label: Overview
sections.paragraph: Epithelial ovarian, fallopian-tube and primary peritoneal cancers arise in closely related tissues and are treated using overlapping approaches. Histological subtype, stage and prior response to platinum chemotherapy influence the treatment question. Repurposing research includes itraconazole in recurrent ovarian clear cell carcinoma, a specific subtype that can respond poorly to cytotoxic treatment. The selected itraconazole report concerns only nine patients with recurrent or persistent clear cell carcinoma. They received the drug with chemotherapy, not as an isolated treatment. This matters within the broader condition because related epithelial cancers still include different histological and molecular groups. A response observed in a small recurrent clear cell series cannot identify benefit for every ovarian or fallopian-tube tumor. The repurposing question is therefore an additional combination strategy in a defined setting, while established care and biomarker-directed approaches retain their separate roles. The report does not test replacement of surgery or platinum-based treatment.

sections.paragraph: A retrospective series combined itraconazole with chemotherapy in nine patients with recurrent or persistent clear cell carcinoma. Responses were observed, but all patients received combination treatment and there was no randomized chemotherapy-only group. The selected combination result is preliminary: the reported response rate was 44%, with a wide 95% confidence interval from 12% to 77%. Without a chemotherapy-only comparator, the contribution of itraconazole cannot be separated from chemotherapy or patient selection. Nor does this establish a single-drug regimen. The studied population was recurrent or persistent ovarian clear cell carcinoma, rather than every epithelial ovarian or fallopian-tube cancer. The proposed strategy should therefore retain its exact combination and subtype context. The comparison therefore describes a selected combination regimen rather than the effect of itraconazole as an independently tested intervention. The fenbendazole profile covers its separate ovarian-cancer research.

sections.label: Safety
sections.paragraph: The itraconazole series concerns nine people with recurrent or persistent ovarian clear cell carcinoma who received itraconazole together with cytotoxic chemotherapy. Safety therefore concerns the complete combination rather than itraconazole in isolation. The chemotherapy regimen and the tolerability of adding another drug both matter when interpreting this report. Because every patient received combination treatment, there was no chemotherapy-only group to identify an incremental toxicity attributable to itraconazole. The small retrospective series also cannot characterize uncommon harms reliably. Observed tumor responses do not resolve those safety uncertainties. The selected study concerns a specific recurrent cancer subtype, so it does not provide a general safety estimate for every ovarian, fallopian-tube or primary peritoneal cancer treatment setting.

The report thus cannot rank itraconazole against established treatment pathways or show that a response signal from this combination applies across all related epithelial cancer subtypes.

guide.title: Glioblastoma
guide.description: Why glioblastoma researchers are testing existing drugs, including mebendazole, alongside standard treatment.

sections.label: Overview
sections.paragraph: Glioblastoma is an aggressive glioma that infiltrates brain tissue, making complete removal difficult even when surgery is feasible. Care commonly combines surgery with radiation and chemotherapy; research on repurposed medicines asks whether another drug can improve that treatment rather than replace it. Mebendazole was tested with temozolomide in a phase 1 study of 24 people with high-grade gliomas, including 18 with glioblastoma. Its purpose was dose, exposure and tolerability assessment, without a randomized temozolomide-only comparator. Other clinical records concern recurrent disease or different combinations: disulfiram did not significantly improve survival and increased severe adverse events, while an uncontrolled atorvastatin study did not demonstrate improved six-month progression-free survival. These findings need their separate tumor populations, background treatments and endpoints, rather than one general claim that repurposing improves glioblastoma outcomes.

sections.label: Options
sections.paragraph: Mebendazole has been investigated as an addition to chemotherapy, with different studies addressing feasibility and survival. The initial phase 1 study examined drug exposure and tolerability in 24 people with high-grade gliomas; it did not establish an added survival effect against temozolomide alone. A later trial reported nine-month survival of 36.6% with temozolomide plus mebendazole and 45% with lomustine plus mebendazole. Both groups received mebendazole, and neither reached the prespecified 55% benchmark, so the comparison does not isolate its contribution. The other cited clinical approaches were also unsuccessful in demonstrating their intended improvement: disulfiram did not significantly improve survival, and a single-arm atorvastatin study did not demonstrate better six-month progression-free survival. These are distinct clinical questions, not interchangeable evidence of one anticancer effect. The memantine profile covers its separate glioblastoma research.

sections.label: Safety
sections.paragraph: Elevated liver enzymes occurred during the phase 1 mebendazole and temozolomide study and could lead to dose reduction or discontinuation. The much shorter courses used for intestinal parasites do not establish the safety of prolonged combination treatment for a brain tumor. Drug-exposure measurements in that study are relevant to delivery, but the small, mixed high-grade-glioma population limits the precision of its tolerability findings. A separate recurrent-disease trial found grade 3 or higher adverse events in 34% with the disulfiram combination versus 11% in the comparator group, without a significant survival improvement. That is a different regimen and cannot supply a mebendazole adverse-event rate. It does show why the actual combination, severe-event findings and intended benefit must remain together when interpreting a repurposed medicine in glioblastoma care.

guide.title: Fibromyalgia
guide.description: Low-dose naltrexone in fibromyalgia: the pain-processing rationale and the results of a larger placebo-controlled trial.

sections.label: Overview
sections.paragraph: Fibromyalgia causes widespread pain and tenderness, often with fatigue, unrefreshing sleep and difficulty thinking clearly. Research points to altered pain processing rather than a single damaged joint or muscle. Low-dose naltrexone has been studied as a way to change central pain modulation. This rationale has been tested through both clinical pain ratings and laboratory measures of pain processing. Those measurements are related questions, but they are not interchangeable outcomes. In the 99-woman FINAL trial, naltrexone did not demonstrate superior average pain relief over placebo after 12 weeks. A later exploratory analysis from the same trial found a difference in conditioned pain modulation, a test of how one painful stimulus changes the response to another. That change did not track improvement in clinical pain. guide.title: Myalgic encephalomyelitis/chronic fatigue syndrome
guide.description: ME/CFS repurposing evidence: patient-derived immune-cell findings, anecdotal naltrexone responses and unresolved clinical questions.

sections.label: Overview
sections.paragraph: ME/CFS is a disabling multisystem illness marked by reduced ability to carry out usual activities, unrefreshing sleep and post-exertional malaise. Physical or mental effort can cause a delayed worsening of symptoms. Naltrexone research has examined altered signaling in natural-killer immune cells as one possible treatment target. The selected treatment research should be distinguished from the illness definition. A natural-killer-cell study examined TRPM3 channel currents in nine people already taking naltrexone and nine healthy controls. It did not randomize ME/CFS patients to treatment or measure recovery. Three separate patient-compiled case histories described variable symptoms during naltrexone use, including one account of improved pain and sleep without improved function. Those observations do not establish that one immune pathway explains the whole illness. The condition's reduced activity and delayed post-exertional worsening remain clinical concerns that a cell measurement alone cannot resolve.

The official product warning addresses a separate, established risk: naltrexone blocks opioid effects and is contraindicated with opioid analgesics or current opioid dependence. Neither the case histories nor the immune-cell study establishes a validated safe ME/CFS regimen.

guide.title: Compulsive sexual behavior disorder
guide.description: Naltrexone for compulsive sexual behavior disorder: effects on urges, trial outcomes and tolerability.

sections.label: Overview
sections.paragraph: Compulsive sexual behavior disorder involves persistent difficulty controlling repetitive sexual behavior that causes marked distress or impairment. The treatment question concerns control and consequences, rather than the frequency of sexual desire alone. Naltrexone has been investigated because opioid-receptor blockade may reduce the rewarding or urge-driven component of behavior. The selected evidence includes an uncontrolled feasibility study and a randomized comparison with paroxetine and placebo. The latter enrolled 73 men and followed treatment for 20 weeks. Self-reported symptoms improved without clearly separating the randomized groups, while interviews favored active treatment on some behavioral outcomes. These different measurements explain why reports can describe improvement without establishing a consistent advantage across outcomes. The studies concern compulsive behavior and its consequences; they do not establish that sexual desire itself is a disorder or that one medicine is preferable for everyone with CSBD.

sections.label: Overview
sections.paragraph: PGAD/genitopelvic dysesthesia involves unwanted genital arousal sensations that persist or recur without corresponding sexual desire. Symptoms can be distressing and are not evidence of unusually high libido. Neurological studies investigate sensory signaling from the genital area, pelvis and sacral nerves, rather than assuming a single psychological or behavioral cause. The distinction shapes both evaluation and treatment research. A person can experience unwanted genital sensations without wanting sexual activity; measuring sexual desire or repetitive behavior alone would miss that defining feature. The neurological case series included medication-associated symptoms and underlying nerve or spinal pathology, while the iPGAD case-control study examined clinical characteristics. These designs help investigate possible contributors rather than establish a single cause for every person. They also do not demonstrate that naltrexone relieves the sensations. Trials of that medicine in compulsive sexual behavior address impaired control of behavior, which is a different condition and cannot be used as a substitute PGAD treatment result.

guide.title: Treatment-resistant depression
guide.description: Pramipexole augmentation for treatment-resistant depression, including the dopamine rationale and randomized trial evidence.

sections.label: Overview
sections.paragraph: Treatment-resistant depression describes continuing depressive illness despite adequate treatment attempts. Its symptoms can include loss of pleasure, motivation and daily function as well as persistent low mood. Pramipexole, originally used for movement disorders, has been studied as an addition to existing antidepressants. The PAX-D investigation concerns treatment-resistant unipolar depression, rather than all depressive conditions or a replacement for existing antidepressants. Its augmentation design added pramipexole to ongoing treatment and compared that addition with placebo. At 12 weeks, depressive symptoms improved more with active augmentation, but adverse effects also led to more treatment stops. This defines a specific benefit and tolerability question. It does not determine whether pramipexole alone is effective, whether the same balance applies to bipolar depression or how it ranks against another active augmentation option. The dopamine rationale addresses reward and motivation without identifying one biochemical cause of every participant's illness. The published correction has not been reconciled, so the presently usable finding retains Low confidence and its numerical interpretation remains provisional.

The benefit came with adverse effects, making both symptom change and tolerability relevant. This concerns the trial's 12-week depressive-symptom endpoint and its augmentation strategy, not pramipexole used alone. Adverse-event discontinuation was also higher, at 20% versus 5% with placebo. Both findings are relevant to understanding the option. PAX-D did not directly compare pramipexole with ketamine, electroconvulsive therapy or another augmentation medicine, and it does not establish that the same outcome applies to bipolar depression. The greater average reduction in depressive symptoms at 12 weeks must therefore be considered alongside the greater frequency of adverse-event discontinuation in the active-treatment group. guide.title: Periodontitis
guide.description: Doxycycline as a periodontal host-response treatment, and how its benefit differs from dental cleaning or antibiotic dosing.

sections.label: Overview
sections.paragraph: Periodontitis involves inflammation and destruction of the tissues and bone that support teeth. Bacterial plaque initiates the problem, while the body's inflammatory response contributes to tissue damage; removing plaque and influencing the host response therefore address related but different parts of the disease. Subantimicrobial-dose doxycycline has been investigated to inhibit tissue-degrading host enzymes alongside scaling and root planing. A multicenter study found additional improvement in clinical attachment and periodontal pocket depth when the medicine was added to the same mechanical treatment given to the control group. Rapamycin research addresses another host-response hypothesis, but its periodontal bone findings came from aged female mice. An animal bone response cannot establish a human periodontal regimen or substitute for the clinical evidence and local care relevant to people with periodontitis.

sections.label: Options
sections.paragraph: Doxycycline was tested as an adjunct to scaling and root planing, rather than as a replacement for cleaning. The multicenter trial analyzed 209 patients over nine months and found greater clinical attachment gain and pocket-depth reduction with subantimicrobial-dose doxycycline than with placebo alongside the same dental treatment. Its proposed target is matrix metalloproteinase activity: these host enzymes can degrade connective tissue, so the intended role differs from using an antibiotic course to eradicate bacteria. The rapamycin record concerns periodontal bone preservation or recovery in aged mice, without a human effect estimate, validated dose or established durability. These interventions therefore occupy different evidence settings. The clinical doxycycline finding is an additional periodontal-measurement benefit during mechanical care; the rapamycin finding is a preclinical observation requiring separate human investigation.

sections.label: Safety
sections.paragraph: Smoking and uncontrolled local plaque remain important influences on periodontal healing and disease progression. A medicine intended to modify the inflammatory response does not remove those local risks or reverse the need to address the bacterial plaque that initiates disease. Continued inflammation can damage the supporting tissues and bone even when an adjunct is part of care. The doxycycline trial followed people receiving the medicine or placebo with scaling and root planing, so its treatment experience belongs to that combined periodontal setting. The separate rapamycin experiments involved small groups of aged female mice, not patients receiving a validated periodontal course. Their bone and inflammatory measurements provide no human adverse-event rate or established safe periodontal dose. Those species and treatment-setting distinctions matter when considering the practical limits of the proposed adjuncts.

guide.title: Sirolimus
guide.description: An mTOR inhibitor investigated for periodontal aging and for disrupting cancer growth and resistance pathways.

sections.label: Overview
sections.paragraph: Oral sirolimus is used to prevent kidney-transplant rejection and to treat lymphangioleiomyomatosis. Repurposing studies include several cancer combinations and a mouse study of periodontal aging. These investigations involve distinct biological targets and outcomes. In cancer, inhibiting mTOR is intended to interfere with growth signaling, sometimes alongside an established treatment such as trastuzumab or intensive chemotherapy. The cited ovarian combination trial tests auranofin with sirolimus, rather than sirolimus alone. In periodontal research, eight weeks of rapamycin affected inflammation and bone measures in aged mice, without testing treatment in people with periodontitis. Oral labeled use also requires blood-level monitoring and indication-specific adjustment. Its established transplant and lung-disease roles do not turn all of these experimental settings into approved or interchangeable uses, and a tissue or pathway response does not establish longer survival.

sections.paragraph: Risks include infection, impaired wound healing, high blood lipids, proteinuria and noninfectious pneumonitis. The same immune and growth effects that support established uses also make its safety context consequential. Infection concerns, delayed wound healing and noninfectious lung inflammation address different kinds of harm and should not be collapsed into a single tolerability judgment. High lipid levels and protein in the urine add monitoring concerns beyond immediate symptoms. Labeled oral treatment requires blood-level monitoring and adjustments for its specific indication, while strong CYP3A or P-glycoprotein inhibitors and inducers can substantially alter exposure. A cancer combination or an animal periodontal experiment does not replace those prescribing safeguards. Safety interpretation therefore needs to retain the coadministered medicines, the treatment setting and the separate risks described in the label.

sections.label: Overview
sections.paragraph: Itraconazole is an antifungal with several distinct cancer research programs. The clinical evidence includes small exploratory trials and uncontrolled chemotherapy series; other cancer findings remain preclinical. Itraconazole inhibits fungal ergosterol synthesis, impairing the fungal cell membrane. Its cancer-repurposing rationale involves several different actions: changing growth signals, restricting blood-vessel formation and disrupting mitochondrial energy metabolism. Hedgehog and WNT are signaling pathways involved in cell growth; angiogenesis is the formation of new blood vessels. The evidence ranges from experiments in cells and mice to pathway measurements in human tumors, so the biological explanation needs to be read alongside the model in which it was tested. Small studies found signals of activity in basal cell, prostate and lung cancers, but designs and endpoints differ.

A retrospective report described nine patients with recurrent or persistent ovarian clear cell carcinoma treated with combination chemotherapy and itraconazole; it cannot isolate the antifungal’s contribution. In a 46-man dose-comparison study, 48.0% in the high-dose group and 11.8% in the low-dose group were free of PSA progression at 24 weeks; there was no standard-care control. The 23-person non-small-cell lung-cancer trial found 67% versus 29% progression-free at three months (p=0.11); the small, prematurely closed study leaves substantial uncertainty.

sections.label: Safety
sections.paragraph: Itraconazole can cause gastrointestinal symptoms, but its most consequential hazards concern the heart, liver and interacting medicines. The capsule label describes a negative effect on cardiac contraction and reports of congestive heart failure, including cases outside treatment of fungal nail infection. Serious liver injury, including liver failure and death, has also been reported, sometimes early in treatment and without previously recognized liver disease. Another reported complication is pseudoaldosteronism, which can present with higher blood pressure and low potassium. Some interactions increase other drugs' concentrations enough to cause dangerous rhythm disturbances, while other combinations add cardiac or hepatic stress. The indication-specific cardiac restrictions, formal drug-interaction contraindications and broader precautions have different meanings. Cancer combinations therefore require interpretation of the complete regimen and the actual capsule formulation; a small trial's activity signal does not remove these established product risks.

sections.label: Contraindications
sections.paragraph: Itraconazole capsules are contraindicated for fungal nail infection in patients with ventricular dysfunction, including congestive heart failure or a history of heart failure. The same label treats other indications differently: use in ventricular dysfunction requires a benefit that clearly outweighs the risk. Pregnancy and planned pregnancy are also explicit restrictions for treatment of fungal nail infection. Hypersensitivity to itraconazole is a separate contraindication that is not limited to that indication. In addition, numerous named co-medications are contraindicated because their concentrations or effects can increase dangerously. Examples include simvastatin, lovastatin and oral midazolam; other restrictions depend on kidney or liver function or a specific treatment phase. These distinctions matter when discussing repurposing. An indication-specific restriction cannot simply be presented as a universal ban, while its narrower wording also cannot be interpreted as reassurance that a different investigational use is safe.

sections.label: Interactions
sections.paragraph: Itraconazole inhibits CYP3A4 and can substantially increase exposure to medicines cleared through that pathway. The capsule label lists contraindicated combinations, combinations that are not recommended, and combinations requiring caution or monitoring; these are distinct levels of restriction. Simvastatin, lovastatin and oral midazolam are among the contraindicated examples. Calcium-channel blockers can create both a pharmacokinetic interaction and an additional cardiac effect, with specific agents expressly contraindicated. Acid-suppressing medicines introduce a different problem: reduced stomach acidity can lower absorption of the capsules and reduce itraconazole exposure. Enzyme-inducing drugs can also lower its concentrations. Consequently, a combination can be problematic through excessive exposure, inadequate exposure or added organ toxicity. These mechanisms require interpretation of the individual drugs and formulation, rather than a general claim that all antifungals or all cancer regimens have the same interaction profile.

sections.label: Dosing
sections.paragraph: Itraconazole dosing depends on the infection, product and intended treatment schedule. The capsule label describes different regimens for systemic fungal infections and fungal nail infection, including schedules with different daily doses and durations. Capsules are taken immediately after a full meal because food affects absorption. Reduced gastric acidity can lower their uptake, and the product label discusses this separately from dose selection. The oral solution produces different exposure at the same nominal dose and is not interchangeable with the capsules. Those distinctions are important when reading cancer-repurposing reports, which can use their own schedules and co-treatments rather than a labeled antifungal regimen. Neither a capsule dose used for one infection nor a dose reported in a small oncology trial establishes a general anticancer schedule. Formulation, administration conditions, interacting medicines and the exact trial population must remain attached to any reported dose.

sections.label: Overview
sections.paragraph: Ivermectin is an oral antiparasitic medicine in the avermectin class. Its U.S. tablet label covers intestinal strongyloidiasis, caused by Strongyloides stercoralis, and onchocerciasis, caused by Onchocerca volvulus. These established parasite indications are separate from the COVID-19 and cancer investigations discussed here. The six-day higher-dose ACTIV-6 trial did not shorten sustained recovery in outpatients with COVID-19, and COVID-OUT did not demonstrate a reduction in its primary composite outcome with ivermectin. Cancer experiments have examined ovarian cancer cells, glioblastoma models, breast cancer models and WNT-TCF-dependent colorectal tumors. Those experiments address biological mechanisms and tumor growth in laboratory systems; they do not establish improved survival, symptoms or quality of life for people with cancer. The cited liver-cancer combination report is retracted and excluded from efficacy conclusions.

In onchocerciasis, inflammatory reactions to dying microfilariae can cause fever, skin symptoms, lymph-node tenderness and eye reactions; the disease and the treatment context affect how these events are interpreted. Postmarketing reports include low blood pressure, seizures, serious skin reactions and liver injury. The label also warns about neurotoxicity, including confusion, impaired consciousness and coma, which has been reported with recommended dosing as well as overdose. Heavy Loa loa infection creates a separate risk of severe or fatal encephalopathy; significant exposure in endemic parts of West or Central Africa calls for assessment before treatment. These label warnings apply independently of whether a repurposing experiment reports an interesting pathway effect.

The US prescribing information notes that the safety of ivermectin in pregnant women has not been established.

sections.label: Contraindications
sections.paragraph: The oral ivermectin tablet label lists hypersensitivity to a product component as its formal contraindication. Several other important restrictions appear as warnings or population-specific precautions instead. Safety has not been established in children weighing less than 15 kg, and the pregnancy section states that use should be avoided because adequate safety evidence is lacking. Exposure to Loa loa is another clinically distinct issue: treatment in people with substantial infection can be associated with serious neurological reactions. The label also describes neurotoxicity reported without that infection and inflammatory reactions associated with dying parasites in onchocerciasis. These situations cannot be reduced to one general allergy warning, but neither should every precaution be mislabeled a formal contraindication. The specific parasite, exposure history, patient population and actual oral product matter when applying these restrictions to the established uses or interpreting a repurposing proposal.

sections.label: Interactions
sections.paragraph: The oral label describes rare postmarketing reports of increased INR when ivermectin was given with warfarin. INR is a measure used to monitor warfarin anticoagulation; this reported interaction is a reason for medication review, rather than evidence that every combination has been tested. The label identifies CYP3A4 as the main enzyme involved in ivermectin metabolism in laboratory studies, but that observation alone does not quantify the clinical effect of every CYP3A4 inhibitor or inducer. A complete interaction assessment for experimental cancer combinations is not on hand in the cited sources. The warfarin signal comes from postmarketing reports rather than a controlled interaction trial with a defined denominator. It therefore does not provide a numerical probability of bleeding or establish that other anticoagulants have the same interaction. The label's description of ivermectin metabolism supplies pharmacological context, while dedicated combination evidence is needed to determine an actual clinical effect for a different interacting medicine.

guide.title: Mebendazole
guide.description: An intestinal-worm medicine studied for disruption of cancer-cell microtubules and migration.

sections.label: Overview
sections.paragraph: Mebendazole treats intestinal worm infections. Cancer research includes ovarian and oral-cell experiments plus glioma combination trials. Mebendazole interferes with parasite tubulin and microtubules, disrupting cellular transport and glucose uptake. In recurrent glioblastoma, neither mebendazole-containing regimen achieved its prespecified survival benchmark. Ovarian and oral-cancer findings cited here are experimental, without corresponding patient survival estimates. Mebendazole was tested in cell lines and patient-derived xenografts; these models assess antitumor activity without establishing a treatment effect in patients. Nine-month survival was 36.6% with temozolomide-mebendazole and 45% with lomustine-mebendazole, below the 55% benchmark; both arms included mebendazole. The oral-cancer cell study found changes in migration and cell-state markers, not clinical tumor response or survival. The glioblastoma trial compared two chemotherapy partners, so it cannot isolate the effect of adding mebendazole to either one.

sections.label: Safety
sections.paragraph: Mebendazole can cause abdominal symptoms during its established anthelmintic use, but higher doses and longer exposure introduce additional concerns. The cited chewable-tablet label reports neutropenia and agranulocytosis with doses or durations beyond those recommended for intestinal worm infections, and recommends blood-count monitoring in those circumstances. Serious skin reactions, including Stevens-Johnson syndrome and toxic epidermal necrolysis, have been reported with concurrent metronidazole. Convulsions have also been reported in infants younger than one year, while the cited product is labeled for children two years and older. Pregnancy requires its own assessment of available human reports, animal findings and the consequences of untreated infection. These distinctions matter for cancer research, where treatment can last longer than a routine deworming course. A short labeled infection regimen cannot establish the safety of repeated high-dose administration or an experimental oncology combination.

guide.title: Fenbendazole
guide.description: A veterinary dewormer with mixed cancer-model findings, unproven human anticancer benefit and documented liver-injury cases.

sections.label: Overview
sections.paragraph: Cancer benefit: Not established. Human anticancer claims remain anecdotal. The human reports cited here describe liver injury rather than controlled cancer treatment. The selected cell and mouse studies have mixed findings and do not establish a human cancer regimen. The positive Dogra 2018 finding concerns slower growth of an A549 lung-cancer xenograft in mice. In contrast, the Duan EMT6 experiments did not improve tumor growth or radiation response with the tested diets and regimens. Gao 2008 reported smaller lymphoma tumors with fenbendazole plus supplemented vitamins, while fenbendazole alone did not significantly differ from control. These model-dependent results cannot establish one anticancer effect across tumor types. Official FDA context is also specific: fenbendazole is not approved for human use, including cancer treatment, and the 2026 generic suspension approval applies to specified parasite infections in cattle and goats.

sections.label: Safety
sections.paragraph: Safety evidence: Low for estimating frequency or individual risk. A 2024 case report described biopsy-confirmed severe liver injury after self-administration, with liver tests returning to normal after cessation. This is a serious human safety signal, but a case report cannot estimate how often it occurs. A separate 2026 report described severe liver injury after a person receiving nivolumab/relatlimab increased self-administered fenbendazole. The authors distinguished suspected drug injury from immune-mediated hepatitis, but the case cannot quantify an interaction or establish a safe combination. Together, the reports concern actual human harm rather than a tested anticancer benefit. Recovery after stopping treatment in one case does not identify a safe threshold for future use, and neither report defines a validated human monitoring schedule. The FDA context remains that fenbendazole is not approved for human use; veterinary approval for specified parasites does not establish human cancer safety.

The concurrent immunotherapy makes attribution clinically important, but a single case cannot determine how either medicine changed exposure to the other. It also cannot establish that lowering a self-administered dose would make the combination safe. The 2024 report separately describes biopsy-confirmed severe liver injury after self-administration, with liver tests normalizing after cessation. guide.title: Guanfacine
guide.description: An alpha-2A agonist investigated with N-acetylcysteine for Long COVID cognitive symptoms.

sections.label: Overview
sections.paragraph: Guanfacine extended release is an ADHD medicine. Its Long COVID evidence includes a small uncontrolled series using combination treatment. The Intuniv product is an extended-release formulation, with an established ADHD indication rather than a Long COVID indication. Guanfacine stimulates central alpha-2A receptors and can lower blood pressure and heart rate, although the label says the mechanism of ADHD benefit is unknown. The Long COVID series combined it with N-acetylcysteine to investigate cognitive symptoms. Eight of twelve participants reported improvement, while four stopped, including two with hypotension or dizziness. Without placebo or a single-drug comparison, that report cannot isolate guanfacine's contribution or establish how commonly cognitive improvement would occur with treatment in a broader Long COVID population. Immediate-release and extended-release guanfacine are not interchangeable milligram for milligram.

sections.label: Benefits
sections.paragraph: Clinical evidence: Low. In an open-label series, eight of twelve people reported cognitive improvement with guanfacine plus N-acetylcysteine. Four stopped treatment: two for unspecified reasons and two for hypotension or dizziness. There was no placebo group or single-drug comparison, so the report cannot isolate guanfacine's effect or predict how often patients will improve. The reported signal concerns cognitive symptoms during combination treatment with N-acetylcysteine, rather than guanfacine used by itself. That distinction leaves the contribution of each component unresolved. Improvement reported by eight participants does not provide a placebo-adjusted response rate, and the four discontinuations must remain part of the account rather than disappearing from interpretation. In particular, two people stopped for hypotension or dizziness, linking tolerability to the observed experience. The series supplies preliminary clinical observations, with Low confidence for estimating benefit. It does not establish a validated treatment for Long COVID or show that the ADHD indication predicts cognitive recovery after infection.

sections.label: Safety
sections.paragraph: Guanfacine can cause sleepiness, fatigue, dizziness and reductions in blood pressure and heart rate. The extended-release label describes orthostatic hypotension, bradycardia and fainting, making the patient's cardiovascular setting and co-medications important. Sedation can be increased by other centrally acting depressants, while dehydration or overheating can worsen susceptibility to fainting. Abrupt discontinuation introduces a different hazard: blood pressure and heart rate can rise, and clinically significant rebound hypertension has been reported. The label therefore describes gradual discontinuation and monitoring rather than treating stopping as a harmless reversal of treatment. These concerns remain relevant when guanfacine is investigated for cognitive symptoms outside its labeled indication. A small clinical series cannot determine the frequency of uncommon cardiovascular events or establish that every release formulation and combination is tolerated. Dose, release characteristics, other medicines and follow-up remain part of the safety interpretation.

sections.label: Contraindications
sections.paragraph: The cited extended-release guanfacine label contraindicates use after a hypersensitivity reaction to the product, its inactive ingredients or another guanfacine-containing product. Its cardiovascular and sedating effects are addressed separately as warnings and precautions. Low blood pressure, slow heart rate, a history of fainting and conditions that can be worsened by those effects require particular attention; they are not all presented as additional formal contraindications. Medicines that lower blood pressure or heart rate can change that assessment, as can other sedating drugs. Abrupt withdrawal is another distinct concern because rebound hypertension can occur after discontinuation. These categories should remain separate when reading off-label cognitive research. An allergy contraindication, a cardiovascular precaution, an interaction and a trial exclusion do not express the same level or type of restriction, and the label's extended-release product context must be preserved.
