sections.paragraph: Guanfacine exposure can rise with strong or moderate CYP3A4 inhibitors and fall with strong or moderate inducers. The extended-release label gives different dose-adjustment instructions for those situations and for starting or stopping an interacting medicine. Examples include azole antifungals among inhibitors and rifampin among inducers, but the actual agent and its effect on metabolism determine the instruction. Other interactions concern additive physiology rather than altered drug concentrations. Antihypertensives or medicines that slow heart rate can increase hypotension, bradycardia or fainting concerns, while alcohol and other central nervous system depressants can increase sedation. These effects cannot be reduced to one general instruction to avoid all other medicines. The release formulation, current dose and change in the accompanying regimen matter. Cognitive-symptom studies evaluate only their specified combinations and do not establish the safety of arbitrary additional blood-pressure or sedating medicines.

The series had no placebo or guanfacine-only comparison, and two participants stopped because of hypotension or dizziness. It cannot establish an optimal Long COVID schedule or show that increasing a dose produces greater cognitive benefit. The label's formulation distinction is especially relevant when describing treatment: immediate-release and extended-release tablets cannot be substituted milligram for milligram, and the labeled tapering instructions address rebound-hypertension concerns.

guide.title: Maraviroc

sections.label: Overview
sections.paragraph: Maraviroc is used with other antiretroviral medicines for CCR5-tropic HIV-1 infection. Cancer studies investigate whether the same receptor can alter invasion or the local immune response. Maraviroc blocks the human CCR5 receptor, preventing CCR5-tropic HIV-1 from entering susceptible cells. Clinical evidence: Low for cancer treatment. The cited colorectal-cancer paper includes a phase I patient study, so this page is not limited to animal or cell evidence. It reports exploratory tumor and immune findings; the abstract does not provide a controlled survival comparison. This human signal does not establish a comparative cancer benefit or a broadly applicable cancer regimen. The cited work reduced pulmonary metastasis in mice; it did not test prevention of metastasis in patients. It linked CCR5 blockade to macrophage changes and tumor-cell death, with clinical activity in an early pilot; a randomized survival advantage was not tested.

sections.paragraph: Maraviroc has a boxed warning for liver toxicity, which can occur with allergic features such as rash or other systemic symptoms. The cited label describes serious hypersensitivity reactions and calls for liver-related evaluation before treatment and when clinically indicated. Postural hypotension is another important concern, particularly when kidney impairment increases exposure or other medicines affect blood pressure. The interaction profile also depends on CYP3A-modifying drugs, which can substantially change the amount of maraviroc in the body. These issues are distinct from whether CCR5 blockade is biologically interesting for a proposed new condition. guide.description: An antibiotic with a separate periodontal use; COVID-19 and cancer investigations test different biological effects.

sections.label: Overview
sections.paragraph: Doxycycline combines antibacterial action with investigated effects on inflammation and tumor biology. Its established antibacterial action inhibits protein production at bacterial 30S ribosomes. A separate low-dose periodontal product targets host collagenase activity and is used with scaling and root planing. These uses should not be conflated with the acute-COVID or cancer questions. PRINCIPLE did not find a clinically meaningful improvement in community COVID-19 recovery or related hospitalization or death. Cancer work has examined tissue markers, invasion, apoptosis and experimental tumor growth rather than demonstrating a survival advantage. Thus the repurposing landscape includes an adjunctive periodontal role, a negative outpatient viral-illness trial and tumor hypotheses that retain their distinct experimental endpoints. The preoperative breast pilot measured CD44 and ALDH1 rather than patient survival.

Its target is tissue breakdown, which is a different purpose from treating a susceptible bacterial infection. In PRINCIPLE, higher-risk community patients with acute COVID-19 had no clinically meaningful improvement in recovery or COVID-related hospitalization or death. sections.label: Safety
sections.paragraph: Doxycycline can cause gastrointestinal symptoms, photosensitivity and irritation or ulceration of the esophagus, while antibiotic exposure can also be associated with Clostridioides difficile diarrhea. The cited label separately addresses effects on developing teeth and bone during pregnancy and childhood, intracranial hypertension and serious hypersensitivity reactions. These hazards have different mechanisms and should not be reduced to one statement about stomach upset. Administration conditions matter: the tablet or capsule form is taken with adequate fluid to reduce esophageal injury, and mineral-containing products can alter absorption. The dose, duration and purpose also differ between conventional antibacterial treatment and the lower-dose periodontal regimen discussed elsewhere. A clinical finding in one of those settings does not establish the safety of every longer course or combination. Interpretation should retain the actual formulation, patient population, accompanying medicines and source-specific adverse-event findings.

Antacids containing aluminum, calcium or magnesium, iron preparations and bismuth subsalicylate can impair absorption, so the accompanying product and its administration timing matter. sections.label: Overview
sections.paragraph: Disulfiram’s alcohol-deterrent action is distinct from its copper-dependent anticancer chemistry. Disulfiram inhibits aldehyde dehydrogenase, causing acetaldehyde to accumulate after alcohol consumption and produce an aversive reaction. The recurrent glioblastoma trial found no significant six-month survival advantage from adding disulfiram and copper to chemotherapy, while severe adverse events increased. The recurrent-glioblastoma randomized trial did not demonstrate a significant survival improvement with the added disulfiram-copper regimen. Breast, melanoma, lung, prostate, and colorectal investigations involve different tumor biology and experimental settings. The mechanistic reports describe tumor-cell effects rather than a shared survival benefit. The glioblastoma study randomized 88 patients and compared the added regimen with chemotherapy alone. This is more direct clinical evidence than tumor-cell experiments.

sections.label: Safety
sections.paragraph: Disulfiram can cause a severe reaction with alcohol, including vomiting, hypotension, breathing difficulty, arrhythmias, collapse and, in serious cases, death. The warning is not limited to a deliberate alcoholic drink: the label also discusses alcohol-containing preparations and disguised exposure. Susceptibility can persist after disulfiram has been stopped because recovery from its enzyme effect takes time. Separate toxicities include hepatitis, peripheral neuropathy and neurological or psychiatric reactions, so avoiding alcohol does not replace monitoring for other adverse effects. The product must not be administered secretly or while a patient is intoxicated; informed understanding of the reaction is part of its labeled context. These issues remain relevant when laboratory anticancer mechanisms motivate repurposing studies. A cell experiment or a combination containing copper does not establish the safety of a human regimen, and the actual dose, co-medications, liver status and clinical follow-up must remain attached to any study.

These combination restrictions are distinct from the broader caution required in conditions such as liver impairment, epilepsy or kidney disease. A person with a history of rubber contact dermatitis may need assessment for sensitivity to thiuram compounds, rather than having that history automatically treated as proof of an allergy to every related substance. The label also requires the patient's knowledge and warns against administration during alcohol intoxication. Changing the proposed treatment goal to cancer does not remove these restrictions, and a research protocol's eligibility rules do not substitute for the actual product's contraindication and interaction assessment.

The label extends the concern to alcohol-containing preparations and explains that reactions can occur after disulfiram itself has been discontinued. Metronidazole and paraldehyde are separately listed among substances that preclude treatment in the specified circumstances. Other interactions can alter the response to medicines such as phenytoin, oral anticoagulants or isoniazid, with different monitoring and toxicity concerns. These relationships should remain distinct rather than being summarized as one nonspecific liver interaction. The complete medication and exposure history therefore matters, including products that are not normally thought of as alcoholic drinks. A proposed anticancer combination does not establish that those interactions are absent or that a laboratory copper-disulfiram exposure reproduces the pharmacology of every oral clinical regimen.

sections.label: Dosing
sections.paragraph: The disulfiram label describes an oral initiation phase followed by a maintenance schedule tailored to the clinical response in its alcohol-dependence treatment setting. Administration is linked to a period without alcohol and to the patient's informed understanding of the disulfiram-alcohol reaction. The drug is one part of a broader management program, rather than a stand-alone way to make alcohol exposure harmless. The source also separates routine dosing from the persistence of alcohol sensitivity after treatment has stopped. Those schedules cannot be relabeled as an established anticancer regimen. Repurposing studies can use different treatment durations, accompanying medicines or experimental combinations, each requiring its own clinical evidence. The nominal daily milligrams therefore need to remain connected to formulation, timing, treatment purpose and monitoring. Neither an approved addiction-treatment dose nor an active laboratory concentration establishes the dose at which a proposed cancer treatment helps patients.

guide.title: Propranolol
guide.description: A beta blocker being studied for the effects of stress signaling on cancer progression.

sections.label: Overview
sections.paragraph: Propranolol blocks adrenergic signaling in cardiovascular use and tumor investigations. Its original action blocks beta-1 and beta-2 adrenergic receptors, reducing the effects of catecholamine signals on the heart and other tissues. Cancer research asks a different question: whether interrupting stress-hormone signaling changes tumor invasion or the immune environment. A randomized breast study tested a brief presurgical course and measured tumor-tissue biology rather than long-term survival. A nine-patient melanoma study combined propranolol with pembrolizumab and primarily addressed dose selection. Pancreatic and prostate work adds experimental signaling hypotheses rather than one established clinical anticancer indication. The original cardiovascular action, a tissue-marker response and a combination-treatment response therefore need to remain separate when interpreting why propranolol is being studied beyond its established uses.

sections.label: Benefits
sections.paragraph: A breast trial found short-term tumor-marker changes. A nine-patient melanoma combination study reported responses, but its single-arm design cannot isolate propranolol’s contribution. The breast comparison measured changes in mesenchymal gene expression and immune-cell markers during a short period before surgery. Those tissue observations do not demonstrate that patients live longer or avoid recurrence. In melanoma, seven of nine patients responded to propranolol plus pembrolizumab, with no dose-limiting toxicity reported, but the main aim was dose selection. Without a pembrolizumab-only control, the responses cannot establish the extra benefit of beta blockade. A promising response proportion in a very small combination study is therefore different from a randomized incremental treatment effect. Both reports are clinically relevant investigations, but each requires its actual endpoint and design limitation rather than a broad claim that propranolol improves cancer outcomes.

sections.label: Safety
sections.paragraph: Propranolol can cause bradycardia, hypotension, and bronchospasm. Abrupt withdrawal can worsen angina; beta blockade can mask warning signs of hypoglycemia. These risks follow from cardiovascular and airway effects that remain relevant when the research goal is cancer treatment. A slow heart rate or low blood pressure is not the same problem as bronchospasm, and beta blockade can also conceal warning signs of low blood glucose. The label lists bronchial asthma, cardiogenic shock, sinus bradycardia and greater-than-first-degree heart block as contraindications. Verapamil or diltiazem can compound slowing of heart rate and conduction, while other blood-pressure-lowering medicines can add hypotension. The nine-patient melanoma study reported no dose-limiting toxicity, but that small selected combination cohort cannot overturn these established restrictions or precisely estimate uncommon adverse events.

The practical issue is overlap between propranolol's beta-blocking effects and the cardiovascular effects of its partner medicine. A combination that slows conduction raises a different concern from one that mainly lowers blood pressure, even when both can affect tolerability. These interactions sit alongside the label's contraindications for sinus bradycardia, significant heart block, cardiogenic shock and bronchial asthma. The melanoma study combined propranolol with pembrolizumab in only nine patients; its lack of dose-limiting toxicity cannot validate every additional co-medication or establish that all beta-blocker combinations have the same safety profile.

sections.paragraph: The breast trial administered propranolol during the week before surgery, a brief perioperative strategy rather than prolonged cancer treatment. Its purpose was to measure changes in tumor gene expression and immune-cell markers within that presurgical window. The schedule therefore does not establish how long a person would need beta blockade to alter recurrence or survival, because those were not the measured endpoints. The melanoma investigation instead used dose escalation with pembrolizumab, primarily to select a dose and examine tolerability in nine patients. Those are distinct study strategies, and a regimen from one cannot be assumed effective in the other. Immediate-release and extended-release propranolol products also have different release profiles. The formulation, timing, partner treatment and intended endpoint must therefore remain attached to a study schedule rather than turning brief exposure into a validated prolonged anticancer course.

Neither supplies a definitive comparative survival effect for adding propranolol to cancer treatment.

guide.title: Simvastatin
guide.description: A cholesterol-lowering statin tested in cancer and vitiligo, with negative results in specific randomized studies.

sections.label: Overview
sections.paragraph: Simvastatin reduces cholesterol and cardiovascular risk in its established uses. Repurposing studies test effects on tumor metabolism and immune-mediated pigment loss. Its established lipid effect follows inhibition of HMG-CoA reductase and reduced hepatic cholesterol production. Repurposing research goes beyond cholesterol outcomes, asking about tumor-cell metabolism or immune responses affecting pigment-producing melanocytes. The pancreatic trial randomized 114 patients to simvastatin or placebo alongside gemcitabine and did not show an efficacy advantage. A small oral vitiligo trial also found no repigmentation benefit. Myeloma work remains cell-line evidence, including reduced viability and decreased IL-6 secretion in U266 cells. These distinct negative clinical comparisons and laboratory observations should remain separate rather than being combined into a general claim of tumor or skin benefit.

Those laboratory effects do not overturn the negative clinical results or establish an effective cancer dose.

sections.label: Safety
sections.paragraph: Simvastatin can cause muscle injury ranging from symptoms with elevated creatine kinase to rhabdomyolysis, which can produce kidney injury and has rarely been fatal. Risk is affected by dose, interacting medicines, kidney impairment and other patient characteristics, rather than being uniform across every regimen. The label also describes liver-related precautions and rare immune-mediated necrotizing myopathy, a condition that can persist after the drug is discontinued. These hazards are different from ordinary transient muscle discomfort and require their own interpretation. The highest-dose regimen has particularly restrictive labeling because muscle toxicity increases with exposure. Repurposing studies in neurological or other conditions therefore cannot be judged solely by the drug's established cholesterol-lowering role. Their actual dose, duration, comorbidities and co-medications must remain explicit, and a disease-specific efficacy finding does not establish the safety of a different or more intensive simvastatin regimen.

sections.label: Contraindications
sections.paragraph: The cited simvastatin label contraindicates use with strong CYP3A4 inhibitors and with specific additional medicines, including cyclosporine, danazol and gemfibrozil. Those combinations can increase exposure or muscle-injury risk through different pharmacological relationships. Acute liver failure, decompensated cirrhosis and hypersensitivity to simvastatin or its excipients are also formal contraindications. Other patient factors and co-medications may require dose limits, monitoring or a different treatment choice without being listed as the same categorical prohibition. This distinction is important because an interaction that requires a dose cap is not identical to a contraindicated combination. The product's high-dose restrictions are another separate issue. When simvastatin is investigated outside lipid lowering, the new treatment goal does not remove these existing boundaries, and exclusions used by an individual trial do not automatically define the full regulatory contraindication list.

sections.paragraph: Simvastatin exposure can increase when CYP3A4 metabolism or relevant transport pathways are inhibited, raising the risk of myopathy and rhabdomyolysis. The label therefore distinguishes prohibited combinations from combinations with specific dose limits or additional precautions. Strong CYP3A4 inhibitors are contraindicated, as are cyclosporine, danazol and gemfibrozil. Other agents, including certain cardiovascular medicines, require their own product-specific instructions rather than a universal rule for the whole drug class. Grapefruit-related exposure and the effects of other lipid-lowering therapies are also part of the interaction discussion. These mechanisms should be kept separate from a trial's hypothesized neurological or anti-inflammatory benefit. The actual co-medication, simvastatin dose and clinical setting matter when comparing regimens. Absence of an interaction in a small repurposing study does not establish that every enzyme inhibitor, supplement or additional lipid-lowering medicine is compatible with the same dose.

guide.title: Crohn disease
guide.description: How molecular profiles in Crohn’s disease are being used to identify new treatment candidates.

sections.label: Overview
sections.paragraph: Crohn’s disease causes chronic inflammation in the digestive tract, with symptoms such as diarrhea, abdominal pain and weight loss. Treatment aims to control inflammation and maintain remission. Disease location, activity, complications and response to previous treatment affect the meaning of any proposed intervention. Crohn's can involve different parts of the digestive tract, so one selected molecular dataset does not automatically represent every patient. The repurposing analysis discussed here used gene-expression patterns from anti-TNF-refractory disease to identify possible drugs for further investigation. It nominated vorinostat and clomipramine for different molecular clusters, without administering either medicine or measuring remission. That distinction keeps the clinical goal, controlling intestinal inflammation and maintaining remission, separate from a computational match. A transcriptomic pattern can guide a research hypothesis but cannot show that symptoms, function or the risk of surgery improve after treatment.

sections.label: Options
sections.paragraph: Repurposing research has used gene-expression patterns from people whose Crohn’s disease did not respond to anti-TNF treatment to nominate vorinostat and clomipramine. These are computational candidates; the analysis did not test symptom improvement or remission after taking either drug. The source describes transcriptomes from 327 patients, not 327 people treated with the nominated drugs. Vorinostat was linked to one molecular cluster and clomipramine to another through comparison with compound-expression signatures. Their scores describe the analysis's matching process rather than the probability of remission or an effect size in patients. Both nominations come from the same original analysis and therefore do not constitute two independent clinical trials. The authors noted reliance on one dataset, possible selection bias and the need for experimental confirmation. These candidates provide a way to frame further research in refractory disease while leaving treatment efficacy and clinical safety unestablished.

sections.paragraph: The computational study provides no Crohn’s-specific tolerability results for these candidates. Established care is selected according to disease location, activity, complications and response to previous treatment. No participant received vorinostat or clomipramine as an intervention in the transcriptome analysis. It therefore cannot show how intestinal symptoms, complications or adverse effects would change during either treatment. The 327 patients described in its methods supplied gene-expression data rather than an exposed safety cohort, so their number is not a tolerability denominator. Crohn's disease can affect different digestive-tract locations, and previous treatment response is part of selecting established care. Those clinical differences matter when considering how broadly a molecular candidate might apply. A favorable compound-matching score does not demonstrate safe use in refractory disease or establish that the nominated medicine can replace a treatment chosen for the patient's actual disease characteristics.

guide.title: Head and neck squamous cell carcinoma
guide.description: Valproic acid investigations in head and neck squamous cell cancer, including the toxicity that limited clinical testing.

sections.label: Overview
sections.paragraph: Head and neck squamous cell cancers arise in the surface lining of sites such as the mouth, throat and larynx. Tobacco, alcohol and, for some sites, high-risk HPV infection contribute to risk. These differences matter when considering a repurposing report because one head and neck treatment setting does not represent every tumor in the region. The selected clinical study investigated valproic acid added to cisplatin-based chemoradiation. Its rationale came from gene-regulation and cell-sensitivity work, but clinical delivery was limited by toxicity, particularly marrow suppression and infection. Tumor responses occurred without establishing a favorable benefit and harm balance for the combination. The investigation therefore describes an experimental addition to established treatment components, rather than valproic acid replacing them or a confirmed intervention across all head and neck sites.

That limitation is part of the result, rather than a side issue that can be set aside because responses were seen. The study did not establish a comparative improvement attributable to valproic acid. Earlier cell experiments showed increased cisplatin-related cytotoxicity and altered tumor growth, but those sensitivity findings do not supply a patient survival estimate. This remains an experimental combination strategy whose biological rationale failed to ensure acceptable clinical tolerability, not an established replacement for cisplatin or radiation.

Toxicity constrained delivery of the cisplatin-based chemoradiation regimen and the phase II investigation was curtailed. This is a safety finding about the combination: experience with valproic acid for another indication cannot substitute for tolerability when it is added to chemotherapy and radiation. Tumor responses occurred, but they did not establish a favorable benefit and harm balance in the presence of these delivery problems. The earlier cell experiments asked whether valproic acid increased tumor sensitivity to cisplatin; they could not establish the clinical tolerability of the full regimen. A rationale for sensitizing malignant cells therefore remains separate from evidence that patients can receive the proposed combination acceptably.

guide.title: Prostate cancer
guide.description: Itraconazole research in advanced prostate cancer, with separate PSA and disease-progression outcomes.

sections.label: Overview
sections.paragraph: Prostate cancer begins in the prostate gland. The itraconazole investigation focused on metastatic cancer progressing despite testosterone-lowering treatment, a specific advanced-disease setting. This was a repurposing study of an antifungal, with 46 men assigned to two dose schedules. The higher-dose group showed modest activity, while the lower-dose group closed early for insufficient activity. Among men receiving the higher dose, 48% had no PSA progression at 24 weeks and median progression-free survival was 35.9 weeks. These measurements describe biochemical or clinical disease control, rather than a demonstrated improvement in overall survival. The study had no standard-treatment control, so random assignment between doses does not show superiority to an androgen-receptor treatment or chemotherapy. Its advanced-disease population is central to interpreting the result and should remain attached to the proposed treatment strategy.

These observations concern itraconazole used in men with metastatic prostate cancer progressing despite testosterone-lowering treatment. The study assigned 29 men to the higher-dose group and 17 to the lower-dose group, so its safety information comes from a limited dose-comparison experience. It did not compare treatment against an androgen-receptor medicine or chemotherapy, and consequently cannot establish a relative safety advantage over those alternatives. The electrolyte, blood-pressure and fluid-retention findings also remain separate from the measures of PSA progression and progression-free survival. A signal of anticancer activity does not answer whether those treatment effects provide an acceptable balance. The relevant interpretation keeps the observed adverse effects, small exposed groups and advanced-disease setting together, without extending this experience to other itraconazole regimens.

Median progression-free survival in that group was 35.9 weeks.

guide.title: Non-small-cell lung cancer
guide.description: Itraconazole added to pemetrexed in a small trial of advanced nonsquamous lung cancer.

sections.label: Overview
sections.paragraph: Non-small cell lung cancer includes several types, particularly adenocarcinoma and squamous cell carcinoma. The pemetrexed-itraconazole trial enrolled the nonsquamous subgroup with metastatic disease. That selection is important because a finding in metastatic nonsquamous disease does not describe all lung cancers or every treatment stage. The itraconazole investigation added the antifungal medicine to pemetrexed and enrolled only 23 people before early closure. Its survival estimates were encouraging but uncertain. Other existing repurposing records address separate questions: metformin did not demonstrate progression-free-survival improvement in NRG-LU001, and ALMERA reported worse overall survival in a small trial. Fenbendazole findings concern A549 xenografts in mice, not treated patients. These interventions therefore need to remain distinct by population, background treatment and evidence type rather than being presented as one shared benefit for non-small-cell lung cancer.

sections.label: Options
sections.paragraph: Adding itraconazole to pemetrexed produced encouraging survival estimates in a trial that enrolled only 23 people before stopping early. The small sample makes those estimates uncertain. Median progression-free survival was 5.5 versus 2.8 months, with P=0.089, so the numerical difference did not reach conventional statistical significance. The same small study also reported an overall-survival difference that needs its early-closure limitation. Separate metformin trials do not confirm a broader repurposing benefit: NRG-LU001 did not demonstrate progression-free-survival improvement, while the smaller ALMERA trial reported worse overall survival. The A549 fenbendazole experiment measured xenograft size and weight in mice and cannot supply a human treatment effect. These findings support an intervention-by-intervention reading, preserving an encouraging but unstable itraconazole signal, negative or unfavorable metformin results, and a distinct animal-only fenbendazole hypothesis.

sections.label: Safety
sections.paragraph: The study’s small enrollment limits detection of uncommon harms from adding itraconazole to chemotherapy. The relevant clinical setting was metastatic nonsquamous disease treated with pemetrexed, so the limited tolerability experience cannot establish safety for all lung-cancer regimens. Only 23 people entered before the study closed early, leaving little ability to characterize infrequent problems or compare risks reliably. Separate repurposing findings also require attention to unfavorable outcomes: the small ALMERA study reported worse overall survival with metformin, which cannot be described as evidence that adding a familiar noncancer medicine is harmless. Fenbendazole's A549 mouse experiment provides no human safety estimate at all. Across these investigations, a proposed biological target or a smaller experimental tumor cannot establish the safety of adding the drug to a patient's actual cancer treatment.

guide.title: Breast cancer
guide.description: Metformin’s metabolic rationale and the negative disease-free-survival result of the MA.32 breast-cancer trial.

sections.label: Overview
sections.paragraph: Breast cancer arises in breast tissue and includes tumors with different hormone-receptor and HER2 characteristics. Repurposing research has asked whether changing insulin and metabolism can improve outcomes alongside standard cancer care. That hypothesis was tested directly in MA.32, which enrolled 3,649 participants without diabetes who had high-risk, operable breast cancer. Metformin or placebo was added to standard treatment over a planned five-year period. The trial did not demonstrate an invasive disease-free-survival advantage, despite changes in insulin-related metabolic measures. This distinction matters within a heterogeneous condition: changing a biological measure does not establish a better cancer outcome. The finding concerns metformin as additional cancer treatment in the enrolled population, rather than deciding whether established glucose-lowering therapy should change in a person who also has diabetes.

guide.title: Colorectal cancer
guide.description: Aspirin after surgery for colorectal cancers with selected PI3K-pathway alterations.

sections.label: Overview
sections.paragraph: Colorectal cancer begins in the colon or rectum, and the local treatment setting matters when interpreting a repurposing study. ALASCCA examined an additional medicine after treatment of localized cancer, selecting tumors with particular PI3K-pathway gene alterations rather than enrolling every colorectal cancer. Its aspirin comparison found fewer recurrences in the prespecified PIK3CA hotspot group, while severe adverse events were more common with aspirin. The benefit and harm findings therefore belong to molecularly selected postoperative patients. Other records ask different questions: celecoxib did not significantly improve overall disease-free survival, and metformin's adenoma-recurrence report concerns precancerous lesions with unresolved numerical and missing-data issues. Ivermectin findings are from pathway-dependent xenograft experiments, not a human cancer treatment trial. These distinctions separate recurrence prevention, experimental biology and treatment of established cancer.

sections.label: Options
sections.paragraph: ALASCCA found fewer postoperative recurrences with aspirin in a molecularly selected population. For tumors with prespecified PIK3CA hotspot mutations, estimated three-year recurrence was 7.7% with aspirin and 14.1% with placebo, with a hazard ratio of 0.49 and 95% confidence interval of 0.24 to 0.98. This is not an estimate for all colorectal cancers. Celecoxib's separate overall disease-free-survival comparison was not statistically significant. A small thalidomide combination study likewise found no significant improvement in response or time to progression. The metformin adenoma report addresses a different prevention endpoint and retains unresolved full-text reconciliation issues. Ivermectin inhibited selected colorectal xenografts, but nonresponsive models and the absence of patient outcomes keep that finding experimental. Each intervention therefore requires its own population, endpoint and uncertainty.

sections.label: Overview
sections.paragraph: Pancreatic cancer begins in the pancreas; the metformin trial studied advanced disease. Its purpose was to add a metabolic intervention to gemcitabine and erlotinib. This is different from testing prevention, treating diabetes or preventing recurrence after surgery for localized disease. Both randomized groups received gemcitabine and erlotinib, and the comparison asked whether metformin added a survival advantage. It did not. A separate randomized simvastatin study examined time to progression with gemcitabine and also found no significant improvement. The itraconazole record is a retrospective combination series, so observed responses cannot be assigned to itraconazole alone. These studies involve distinct drugs and background regimens within advanced disease. They should be interpreted by the actual clinical goal and comparator, rather than assuming that a metabolic or antifungal rationale establishes a general pancreatic-cancer benefit.

guide.title: Melanoma
guide.description: Propranolol as an experimental addition to immune checkpoint treatment in melanoma.

sections.label: Overview
sections.paragraph: Melanoma develops from pigment-producing melanocytes. In advanced disease, immune checkpoint drugs and, for eligible tumors, molecularly targeted treatments are important treatment approaches. The repurposing study selected here explored propranolol together with pembrolizumab in nine people with advanced melanoma. Propranolol's proposed effect on adrenergic influences in the immune environment is different from pembrolizumab's checkpoint action. The phase I study primarily examined safety and tolerability and also observed tumor responses. Everyone received the combination, so those responses do not identify an added effect from propranolol. This is an early combination hypothesis within advanced-disease research, not a replacement for established immune or mutation-directed approaches. In particular, the report cannot establish improved response or survival over pembrolizumab alone or generalize to every melanoma treatment setting.

guide.title: Basal-cell carcinoma
guide.description: Itraconazole in basal cell carcinoma: exploratory human tumor and pathway findings, safety signals and missing long-term outcomes.

sections.label: Overview
sections.paragraph: Basal cell carcinoma begins in basal cells in the lower epidermis. It usually grows slowly but can invade surrounding tissue. Itraconazole has been studied because Hedgehog signaling is important in this cancer. The selected clinical study enrolled 29 participants, of whom nineteen received the antifungal in an open-label exploratory program. It examined biological markers as well as short-term tumor area, rather than establishing definitive treatment success. The tumor-area finding has Low clinical confidence and came from a subset assessed for that secondary outcome. It does not show durable cure, prevention of recurrence or superiority to established local treatment. Moderate fatigue and a severe congestive-heart-failure event also occurred during this small study. The repurposing rationale therefore remains tied to its limited treatment experience and measured outcomes, with long-term cancer control and comparative safety unresolved.

Tumor area was a secondary assessment in a subset; the result does not establish durable cure, recurrence prevention or superiority to standard local treatment. Mean tumor area fell by 24%, with a 95% confidence interval from 18.2% to 30.0%, among the treated participants assessed for this outcome. A smaller measured lesion is a different endpoint from proving complete cancer removal or freedom from later recurrence. The study also examined tumor biomarkers to investigate the Hedgehog-pathway rationale, but biological activity cannot substitute for those longer-term clinical outcomes. There was no comparison with curative local treatment or approved Hedgehog-pathway medicines. The finding supports a bounded exploratory observation, while leaving the treatment's comparative value unsettled.

guide.title: Hepatocellular carcinoma
guide.description: Aspirin research on liver-cancer risk in chronic viral hepatitis, distinct from treatment of established cancer.

sections.label: Overview
sections.paragraph: Hepatocellular carcinoma is the most common primary liver cancer and begins in hepatocytes. Chronic hepatitis B or C infection and cirrhosis are important risk contexts. Primary liver cancer is distinct from cancer that begins elsewhere and spreads to the liver. That distinction also separates prevention research from treatment of an existing tumor. The aspirin cohort discussed here followed people with chronic viral hepatitis and examined subsequent hepatocellular-carcinoma incidence, rather than tumor shrinkage after diagnosis. A separate pilot trial tested celecoxib and lanreotide together with transarterial chemoembolization, or TACE, in established disease. Because two drugs were added, its survival difference cannot be assigned to celecoxib alone. These studies therefore address different clinical questions within liver-cancer research, and their populations, intervention combinations and outcomes should remain explicit when considering any proposed repurposed medicine.

sections.label: Options
sections.paragraph: A Swedish observational study associated aspirin use with lower subsequent liver-cancer incidence among people with chronic viral hepatitis. This was prevention research, not a trial treating existing hepatocellular carcinoma. The estimated ten-year incidence was 4.0% among aspirin users and 8.3% among nonusers, with an adjusted hazard ratio of 0.69 and a 95% confidence interval of 0.62 to 0.76. Adjustment addresses measured differences but cannot remove every possible difference between the groups. The association therefore does not establish an individual preventive effect or a treatment for existing cancer. A separate pilot trial reported median survival of 15 versus 7.5 months with TACE plus celecoxib and lanreotide compared with TACE alone. Because that regimen added two medicines, the observed difference cannot identify celecoxib's separate contribution. Prevention and combination-treatment findings remain distinct.

Decisions in people with chronic liver disease must account for bleeding susceptibility alongside any proposed preventive benefit. A lower cancer-incidence association does not remove bleeding as a separate outcome or establish that every person with liver disease has the same balance of risks. The relevant question includes the underlying liver-disease context as well as the proposed preventive purpose. It also differs from tolerability during treatment of an established tumor. The celecoxib pilot added both celecoxib and lanreotide to TACE; its survival finding cannot establish the safety or contribution of either added drug on its own, and cannot resolve aspirin's preventive risk-benefit question.

The celecoxib pilot instead compared TACE with a regimen adding both celecoxib and lanreotide in established disease. Its reported median-survival difference concerns that entire combination and cannot identify celecoxib's independent effect. These are neither the same comparator nor the same disease stage or endpoint. A prevention association should therefore remain separate from a treatment survival result, and neither supplies a direct head-to-head comparison of aspirin and celecoxib as therapies for an existing liver tumor.

guide.title: Multiple myeloma
guide.description: Selected myeloma repurposing research, separating experimental anticancer mechanisms from clot prevention and established treatment context.

sections.label: Overview
sections.paragraph: Multiple myeloma is a cancer of plasma cells in the bone marrow. It can damage bone and interfere with healthy blood-cell production. Thalidomide is an example of repurposing that reached an approved cancer indication. This is a selected-source overview of investigated interventions, not a complete survey of every repurposed drug for myeloma. Experimental tumor studies and clot-prevention research answer different questions. The experimental studies selected here concern metformin, itraconazole with arsenic trioxide and simvastatin in tumor models or cell lines. They should not be interpreted as additional approved treatment options or evidence that those agents improve survival in patients. Aspirin has a different role in the selected human evidence: its comparison with enoxaparin addresses thrombosis prevention during lenalidomide-based therapy. That supportive-care endpoint does not test aspirin's antimyeloma activity. Keeping established cancer treatment, experimental tumor effects and prevention of treatment-associated clots distinct makes the intervention landscape clearer without suggesting that the selected sources are a complete treatment review.

sections.paragraph: The selected experimental candidates below remain distinct from established myeloma treatment. Their laboratory effects do not determine which treatment a patient should receive. Metformin inhibited cell and mouse xenograft growth with AMPK activation, mTOR-related changes, autophagy and cell-cycle arrest; the cell experiments did not show apoptosis. Itraconazole with arsenic trioxide reduced cell growth and mouse tumor burden with lower GLI1-related Hedgehog signaling. That combination cannot establish an itraconazole-alone regimen. Simvastatin reduced viability in myeloma cell lines, with differing cell-cycle and cell-death responses between lines. All three remain model evidence with Low confidence for clinical translation. They are distinct from thalidomide with dexamethasone, which has an established approved indication, and do not identify a human anticancer dose or survival benefit.

sections.label: Safety
sections.paragraph: Thalidomide's clinically important hazards include severe birth defects, blood clots and nerve damage. These risks are integral to treatment selection and monitoring, including when repurposing has led to an approved cancer indication. The established combination with dexamethasone should remain separate from experimental myeloma-cell studies of other drugs. Those laboratory studies do not provide human tolerability estimates or identify effective anticancer doses. Aspirin research in selected patients receiving lenalidomide-based treatment addresses another aspect of safety: prevention of treatment-associated thrombosis. Its comparison with enoxaparin is supportive-care evidence, rather than evidence that aspirin controls myeloma. Keeping these purposes separate prevents a clot-prevention result from being interpreted as either an anticancer benefit or a general safety endorsement for experimental combinations.

sections.label: Comparisons
sections.paragraph: Anticancer benefit: Not established by the aspirin study. Its randomized comparison with enoxaparin concerned clot prevention during lenalidomide-based myeloma treatment. This is human supportive-care evidence, not a test of aspirin as an antimyeloma drug. Different treatment purposes cannot be pooled into one cancer-benefit estimate. The aspirin and enoxaparin comparison instead asks how to prevent treatment-associated thrombosis in a selected clinical population. Its purpose differs from both the approved thalidomide-dexamethasone cancer combination and the experimental tumor effects of metformin, itraconazole combinations or simvastatin. A favorable or comparable clot-prevention finding cannot be used to infer malignant plasma-cell control. Similarly, cell-cycle arrest, growth inhibition or mouse tumor effects do not identify which preventive anticoagulant strategy is appropriate. These separate endpoints explain why the selected studies should not be pooled into one ranking of repurposed myeloma therapies or one estimate of patient cancer benefit.

guide.title: Acute myeloid leukemia
guide.description: Valproate as an addition to decitabine in older adults with acute myeloid leukemia.

sections.label: Overview
sections.paragraph: Acute myeloid leukemia is a fast-growing cancer of blood-forming cells in the bone marrow. Abnormal immature cells increase rapidly and impair normal blood formation, distinguishing its course from slower chronic leukemias. Repurposing studies have explored medicines that alter leukemia-cell gene regulation. The selected randomized trial enrolled older adults considered unsuitable for intensive induction chemotherapy and tested additions to decitabine. It independently assigned valproate and all-trans retinoic acid, allowing the two add-on questions to be evaluated separately. Valproate did not demonstrate a remission or survival advantage. Favorable findings associated with the retinoic-acid assignment therefore cannot be attributed to valproate or the whole list of study medicines. The selected population, ongoing decitabine treatment and separate factorial assignments are central to understanding what this investigation contributes to AML care.

sections.label: Options
sections.paragraph: Adding valproate to decitabine did not demonstrate a remission or survival advantage in the selected older AML population. The reported remission proportions were 17.8% and 17.2%, with an odds ratio of 1.06 and 95% confidence interval of 0.51 to 2.21. That interval does not establish an improvement or exact equivalence. The same factorial trial separately randomized all-trans retinoic acid, and its favorable remission and survival findings belong to that assignment. Participants did not receive valproate instead of decitabine; the clinical question was its additional contribution in people ineligible for intensive induction treatment. A positive finding for the separately assigned medicine cannot reverse the null valproate comparison. Keeping the two additions distinct prevents a multi-drug trial from becoming an unsupported claim that every component improved AML outcomes.

sections.label: Safety
sections.paragraph: The AML trial enrolled older adults considered ineligible for intensive induction chemotherapy, making treatment burden and tolerability especially relevant to its clinical purpose. The absence of a demonstrated valproate survival advantage cannot supply a proven survival gain to offset an additional medicine in that selected population. This is not itself a numerical estimate of valproate toxicity. The related head and neck cancer investigation illustrates why safety remains regimen-specific: valproic acid with cisplatin-based chemoradiation encountered marrow suppression and infections that constrained delivery. Those events occurred in another disease and combination and cannot be assigned as AML adverse-event rates. They also cannot establish that the decitabine combination has the same toxicity. Interpreting suitability therefore requires retaining the actual background treatment and population rather than transferring either favorable or unfavorable tolerability across different oncology regimens.

sections.label: Comparisons
sections.paragraph: The factorial design addressed two additions to decitabine through independent assignments: valproate and all-trans retinoic acid. It therefore provides separate tests of the added medicines, rather than a single comparison in which all favorable findings belong to both. Valproate did not demonstrate a remission or survival advantage, whereas the favorable findings were associated with retinoic acid. The valproate remission proportions, 17.8% versus 17.2%, describe that specific randomized question in older people unsuitable for intensive induction chemotherapy. They do not compare valproate with every AML treatment or establish a replacement for decitabine. Nor can the head and neck chemoradiation experience provide a direct AML efficacy comparison: its disease, partner therapies and delivery problems are different. These distinctions preserve attribution to the actual assignment and regimen tested.

sections.label: Evidence
sections.paragraph: The randomized trial used a factorial design to separate valproate from all-trans retinoic acid while participants received decitabine. This structure matters because favorable findings for retinoic acid cannot be reassigned to valproate merely because both appear in the same report. The valproate comparison showed no remission or survival advantage in older adults ineligible for intensive induction chemotherapy. Its remission odds ratio was 1.06, with a 95% confidence interval from 0.51 to 2.21, indicating uncertainty around a result close to no difference. The study therefore does not establish exact equivalence or a general verdict on every gene-regulating medicine. It addresses an incremental clinical strategy in a defined population; disease biology and a proposed epigenetic rationale cannot substitute for that unsuccessful treatment comparison.

guide.title: Chronic myeloid leukemia
guide.description: Pioglitazone research aimed at deeper molecular responses in chronic myeloid leukemia.

sections.label: Overview
sections.paragraph: Chronic myeloid leukemia involves abnormal myeloid blood cells. Pioglitazone has been studied alongside imatinib to target persistent leukemia cells after an initial molecular response. The ACTIM participants continued imatinib, making this a strategy for residual disease rather than a replacement leukemia treatment. The study used MR4.5, a very deep reduction in BCR::ABL1 transcripts, to assess whether response became deeper. That molecular measurement is different from an ordinary blood count returning to normal and does not itself establish cure or longer survival. Twenty-four patients were evaluable, without a randomized concurrent imatinib-only group. Pioglitazone's proposed action on persistent leukemia cells therefore remains a rationale, while the observed molecular responses have Low confidence for attributing a patient-important benefit to pioglitazone itself. The selected population and continuing background treatment are central to interpreting the finding.

sections.label: Options
sections.paragraph: The ACTIM study reported deep molecular responses after adding pioglitazone to imatinib. Its single-arm design cannot establish how many responses were caused by pioglitazone rather than continued imatinib treatment. ACTIM enrolled people whose CML was already responding to long-term imatinib, but had not reached the study's deeper molecular-response target. It therefore examined an add-on strategy for residual disease, rather than pioglitazone as a replacement for a leukemia medicine. Twenty-four patients were evaluable. The estimated cumulative incidence of reaching MR4.5 by 12 months was 56%, with a 95% confidence interval of 37% to 76%. The confidence interval is wide, and continuing imatinib could contribute to deeper responses over time. MR4.5 identifies very low leukemia-associated RNA rather than a demonstrated survival advantage, cure or permission to stop imatinib; the authors called for randomized confirmation.

questions.answer: No. Participants continued imatinib, and the question was whether adding pioglitazone could deepen an existing molecular response.

sections.label: Safety
sections.paragraph: Edema led one ACTIM participant to stop pioglitazone. Fluid retention is especially relevant when adding this medicine to an ongoing cancer regimen. The main report also describes weight gain and a reduction in hemoglobin during treatment. Pioglitazone exposure varied because several participants stopped early after a regulatory concern about bladder cancer. These observations qualify the interpretation of tolerability and do not establish the safety of adding pioglitazone to every CML regimen. The population already had a response to long-term imatinib and remained on that medicine. Safety observations therefore concern an add-on approach, not pioglitazone alone. Early discontinuation also limits what the small study can show about prolonged exposure, especially for uncommon or delayed adverse effects. The 24 evaluable participants supplied a limited treatment-exposure experience within this continuing imatinib regimen.

sections.paragraph: ACTIM did not include a randomized imatinib-only group. Historical response rates offer context but cannot provide an equally reliable treatment comparison. Participants continued their established imatinib treatment, and a separate imatinib-only cohort was nonrandomized. Differences in patient characteristics or additional time on imatinib could therefore contribute to apparent differences in deep molecular response. The observed 56% estimated cumulative incidence of MR4.5 at 12 months is not the percentage proven to benefit because of pioglitazone. Its 95% confidence interval, 37% to 76%, also reflects substantial uncertainty in this small study. The comparison concerns a molecular target among patients with residual disease after response, rather than first-line replacement therapy, cure or survival. A randomized add-on comparison would be needed to separate pioglitazone's contribution more reliably from the background treatment.

guide.title: Atorvastatin
guide.description: A cholesterol-lowering statin investigated for cancer-cell metabolism and vitiligo inflammation.

sections.label: Overview
sections.paragraph: Atorvastatin has established lipid-lowering and cardiovascular indications. Repurposing trials include negative overall prostate biomarkers and no added vitiligo benefit with phototherapy. Its original action inhibits HMG-CoA reductase, reducing cholesterol synthesis in the liver and increasing LDL clearance. Repurposing studies instead ask whether related growth and inflammatory pathways affect tumors or pigment-cell loss. These clinical questions do not inherit the established cardiovascular benefit. The prostate and breast studies used short treatment windows before surgery and measured tissue proliferation rather than recurrence or survival. The glioblastoma investigation was a single-arm combination study, while the AML report involved leukemia cell lines. Together with the unsuccessful vitiligo add-on comparison, these records show why a shared metabolic rationale must remain separate from evidence that atorvastatin improves a particular noncardiovascular patient outcome.

guide.title: Rituximab
guide.description: A B-cell-depleting antibody explored in a very small vitiligo pilot.

sections.label: Overview
sections.paragraph: Rituximab is used in specified B-cell cancers and autoimmune diseases. Its vitiligo evidence includes an uncontrolled five-person pilot. The established action is depletion of CD20-positive B cells, a target relevant to its specified cancer and autoimmune indications. The vitiligo rationale instead asks whether reducing B-cell contributions and autoantibodies could lessen injury to pigment-producing melanocytes. The five-person pilot used one 1 g intravenous infusion and six months of follow-up. Three participants had clear clinical and histological improvement, one slight improvement and one no change. These uncontrolled observations remain preliminary and do not establish an average effect or retreatment schedule. The infusion, infection and other serious labeled risks remain relevant even though the investigated condition is a pigment disorder.

sections.label: Benefits
sections.paragraph: Clinical evidence: Low. An uncontrolled vitiligo pilot treated five people with one rituximab infusion and followed them for six months. Three showed clear clinical and histological improvement, one slight improvement and one no change. Without a control group, this does not establish an average treatment effect, durability beyond follow-up or a validated retreatment schedule. Clinical appearance and skin-biopsy changes were recorded in the same five participants, so they should not be counted as separate clinical trials. The three clear improvements, one slight improvement and one unchanged case describe the range observed after a single infusion. They do not establish what would have happened without treatment or what proportion of a broader vitiligo population would benefit. The report also cannot show whether improvement persists beyond six months or whether further infusions are useful. These limits leave clinical evidence Low and keep the autoimmune rationale distinct from a demonstrated, durable, comparatively estimated effect on pigmentation.

sections.label: Safety
sections.paragraph: Label context: Boxed warnings cover fatal infusion reactions, severe mucocutaneous reactions, hepatitis B reactivation and progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy. The label requires hepatitis B screening and baseline blood counts. Infusions need trained staff and support for serious reactions; infection surveillance continues during and after treatment. These precautions apply even when an investigated condition is not cancer. Severe infusion reactions can include breathing difficulty, hypotension and cardiac complications, particularly during early exposure. Hepatitis B reactivation is another specific risk, so the label describes screening and monitoring separately from management of an infusion reaction. Progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy, serious infections and tumor lysis syndrome involve different mechanisms and patient settings. The risks depend on the disease, circulating malignant-cell burden, accompanying immunosuppression and the actual infusion regimen, rather than simply the fact that B cells are depleted.

sections.paragraph: The cited rituximab label lists no formal contraindications, but it contains extensive warnings that strongly constrain clinical use. These include potentially fatal infusion reactions, severe mucocutaneous reactions, hepatitis B reactivation and progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy. Serious infections, tumor lysis and cardiovascular complications require additional assessment in their respective settings. The label's hepatitis B screening and monitoring requirements are different from a formal contraindication list, as are precautions concerning active infection, vaccination and concurrent immunosuppression. This classification should not be collapsed into the misleading conclusion that a medicine with no listed contraindications is broadly safe for any proposed indication. Equally, an exclusion in a small repurposing study is not automatically a new regulatory contraindication. The actual product, disease, immune status, co-treatment and infusion setting define the context in which these substantial risks must be interpreted.

It nevertheless reports specific pharmacokinetic observations: rituximab did not change systemic exposure to fludarabine or cyclophosphamide in the cited CLL setting, and methotrexate or cyclophosphamide did not change rituximab pharmacokinetics in rheumatoid arthritis trials. Those findings address measured drug exposure, not the complete safety of every immunosuppressive combination. Infection risk and the consequences of B-cell depletion remain clinically important even without a demonstrated metabolic interaction. Vaccination is another distinct issue because immune responses can be impaired, and the label addresses vaccination timing and live-virus vaccines separately. A monoclonal antibody's interaction profile therefore cannot be summarized only by the CYP-enzyme framework used for many oral medicines. Evidence for a proposed repurposing combination must retain its actual co-treatments, immune context and clinical outcomes.

sections.label: Overview
sections.paragraph: Celecoxib treats pain and inflammatory conditions through COX-2 inhibition. Large breast and colon trials did not show overall disease-free survival benefit; smaller combination studies address different questions. Celecoxib selectively inhibits COX-2, reducing prostaglandin production involved in pain and inflammation. REACT did not improve breast-cancer disease-free survival, and CALGB/SWOG 80702 did not improve it overall in stage III colon cancer. A PIK3CA-defined colon subgroup and a small liver-cancer combination trial reported favorable findings; the latter cannot isolate celecoxib. Long COVID reports used multiple drugs without randomization. The 24 completers reported symptom improvements on valacyclovir-celecoxib with or without Paxlovid; convenience sampling and multiple drugs prevent attribution to celecoxib. DoCaCel found no significant progression-free or overall survival advantage, with interpretation limited by premature celecoxib discontinuation.

sections.label: Safety
sections.paragraph: Celecoxib retains serious NSAID risks despite its COX-2 selectivity. The label carries boxed warnings for cardiovascular thrombotic events and gastrointestinal bleeding, ulceration or perforation, which can occur without warning symptoms and can be fatal. Cardiovascular risk can occur early and increase with longer exposure, while older age and a history of gastrointestinal bleeding change the risk assessment. Kidney injury, fluid retention, worsening hypertension and liver injury are additional concerns, and serious skin or hypersensitivity reactions require separate attention. Pregnancy-related restrictions also depend on timing and the fetal risks of NSAID exposure. These hazards are not removed by an investigational anti-inflammatory or anticancer rationale. guide.title: Minocycline
guide.description: An antibiotic investigated for inflammation and neuroprotection, with several negative clinical trials and a harmful ALS result.

sections.label: Overview
sections.paragraph: Minocycline is an antibiotic with separate anti-inflammatory research programs. Large trials did not show benefit for mild Alzheimer’s disease or recent-onset schizophrenia, while the ALS trial found faster deterioration. The clinical record therefore does not support a single neuroprotective effect across diseases. MADE tested cognition and daily function over two years in mild Alzheimer's disease and found no benefit. BeneMin addressed recent-onset schizophrenia, while the ALS study observed faster functional-score decline rather than improvement. The early-MS finding concerned conversion after a first demyelinating event at six months; the difference was not significant at 24 months. Other records involve depression, vitiligo and preclinical ovarian-cancer experiments. Their populations and endpoints differ, so a laboratory anti-inflammatory action or an outcome in one disease cannot establish effectiveness in another. Established antibacterial use also retains its own label-based safety and interaction restrictions.

sections.label: Benefits
sections.paragraph: The most substantial neurological findings are mixed or unfavorable: no benefit in Alzheimer’s disease or BeneMin schizophrenia, and faster functional decline in ALS. An early-MS trial found a six-month effect; the difference was not statistically significant at 24 months; small vitiligo results address disease activity, and ovarian results are preclinical. Six weeks of adjunctive treatment also failed to significantly improve treatment-resistant depression severity in a 168-person analysis. The Parkinson's follow-up assessed feasibility for larger efficacy testing and did not establish slower disease progression. In the 50-person vitiligo comparison, activity decreased with minocycline and dexamethasone without a significant between-group difference, and there was no placebo arm. The ovarian report examined cells and mouse tumors, not patient response. These separate negative, harmful, exploratory and preclinical findings prevent a common anti-inflammatory rationale from being described as an established benefit across conditions.

In MADE, the higher 400 mg daily Alzheimer's regimen was poorly tolerated over the two-year study. In ALS, the problem was more consequential than an incidental adverse symptom: functional scores deteriorated faster with minocycline. Those observations need to remain visible when interpreting the proposed anti-inflammatory or neuroprotective rationale.

sections.label: Overview
sections.paragraph: Hydroxychloroquine has malaria and autoimmune indications; repurposing examines viral entry and autophagy. The cited clinical studies address distinct repurposing questions and do not establish a general benefit from changing intracellular processing. RECOVERY tested hospitalized COVID-19 and found no reduction in 28-day mortality. The 2025 ovarian study added hydroxychloroquine to chemotherapy and found no significant response or survival improvement. Its 59-patient population provided much less survival precision than RECOVERY's thousands of hospitalized participants. Established malaria and autoimmune use also retains separate label risks, including retinal damage, cardiomyopathy, QT prolongation and hypoglycemia. These differences make it necessary to keep the original indications, the proposed experimental targets and the actual patient outcomes separate, rather than assuming that a familiar medicine or a plausible cellular rationale establishes effectiveness in a new disease.

sections.label: Benefits
sections.paragraph: RECOVERY found no reduction in 28-day mortality from hydroxychloroquine in hospitalized COVID-19. A 2025 ovarian trial found no significant response or survival improvement when it was added to chemotherapy. In RECOVERY, deaths occurred in 27.0% of hydroxychloroquine recipients and 25.0% with usual care, with a rate ratio of 1.09 and 95% confidence interval of 0.97 to 1.23. That finding concerns treatment after hospitalization, not prevention of infection. In the ovarian study, response among evaluable patients was 85% versus 80%, a nonsignificant difference with P=0.65. A numerical response difference therefore cannot be described as an established benefit of adding hydroxychloroquine. These trials involve different diseases, background treatments and endpoints, but both require their actual unsuccessful comparisons to remain visible. A proposed effect on intracellular compartments does not replace evidence of improved survival or tumor response.

sections.label: Safety
sections.paragraph: Important risks include retinal damage, cardiomyopathy and QT prolongation, severe skin reactions, and hypoglycemia. Retinal risk depends on exposure and duration. Exposure and duration are particularly important for interpreting retinal risk, rather than treating all courses as equivalent. Cardiac muscle toxicity and QT-related rhythm concerns are separate cardiovascular issues, while low blood glucose can become relevant alongside insulin or another glucose-lowering medicine. The label also describes severe skin reactions and identifies hypersensitivity to 4-aminoquinoline compounds as a contraindication. Co-medications can add risk: other QT-prolonging drugs raise arrhythmia concerns, and digoxin concentrations can increase. These established restrictions remain relevant when hydroxychloroquine is investigated in hospitalized infection or added to chemotherapy. Neither an antimalarial history nor a proposed cancer mechanism establishes safe use across all of those regimens and treatment durations.

guide.title: Aspirin
guide.description: Aspirin has a mutation-selected colorectal recurrence result; its other cancer and multiple-sclerosis investigations ask different questions.

sections.label: Overview
sections.paragraph: Aspirin investigations span cancer recurrence, cancer prevention, and prevention of treatment-related thrombosis. These purposes are distinct even when the same drug is involved. ALASCCA randomized aspirin after curative colorectal-cancer treatment in tumors selected for PI3K-pathway alterations. The chronic-hepatitis report instead observed first hepatocellular carcinoma diagnoses and may retain residual confounding. In myeloma, a randomized comparison with enoxaparin addressed blood clots during lenalidomide-based treatment, not cancer control. A multiple-sclerosis example is more preliminary still: it analyzed gene-expression signatures without administering aspirin for MS symptoms, relapses or disability. The selected record therefore ranges from a molecularly defined recurrence trial to observational prevention, supportive care and a computational nomination, with separate clinical meanings. Its established action includes inhibition of platelet aggregation.

sections.label: Benefits
sections.paragraph: Aspirin reduced recurrence in mutation-selected colorectal cancer. A hepatitis cohort associated use with lower liver-cancer incidence, while selected myeloma studies address clot prevention. In the PIK3CA exon 9 or 20 hotspot group, three-year recurrence was 7.7% with aspirin and 14.1% with placebo, with a hazard ratio of 0.49. That benefit retains its tumor-mutation eligibility and post-treatment recurrence endpoint. The chronic-hepatitis cohort observed ten-year HCC incidence of 4.0% among aspirin users and 8.3% among nonusers, but an association may reflect residual confounding. In the selected low-risk myeloma comparison, clot rates were 2.27% with aspirin and 1.20% with enoxaparin, without a significant difference. Those clot outcomes do not show an antimyeloma effect, and the computational MS nomination provides no clinical response estimate.

sections.paragraph: Aspirin can cause serious gastrointestinal bleeding and severe allergic reactions, including wheezing, facial swelling or shock. The cited 325-mg tablet label identifies higher bleeding concern with older age, prior ulcers or bleeding, anticoagulants or steroids, other NSAIDs, greater alcohol intake, and doses or durations beyond the directions. Those factors are different from the intended antiplatelet effect and cannot be interpreted as evidence that more platelet inhibition is always beneficial. The label also warns about Reye's syndrome in children or teenagers with chickenpox or flu-like illness and gives a separate pregnancy precaution. Signs such as bloody or black stools, vomiting blood or feeling faint require prompt evaluation rather than being treated as routine indigestion. A prevention or cancer-repurposing study therefore needs its actual dose, formulation, population and follow-up preserved; an efficacy signal does not remove the established bleeding and allergy risks.

Pregnancy restrictions also retain their timing and clinical qualifications. guide.title: Pioglitazone
guide.description: An insulin sensitizer studied for leukemia-cell differentiation and for muscle function during weight loss.

sections.label: Overview
sections.paragraph: Pioglitazone treats type 2 diabetes; additional studies examine leukemia persistence and muscle function during weight loss. Pioglitazone activates PPAR-gamma, a nuclear receptor that changes gene transcription and improves insulin sensitivity in liver and peripheral tissues. ACTIM reported deeper molecular responses after adding pioglitazone to imatinib, without randomization. A separate older-adult trial found enhanced training-related leg-power gains in women but not men. The 24-patient ACTIM chronic myeloid leukemia single-arm phase II study reported 56% cumulative MR4.5 by 12 months. Its comparison cohort was not randomized. The body-composition study attributed reduced thigh muscle loss to resistance training; pioglitazone’s effects were mainly on selected fat compartments. ACTIM was a 24-patient single-arm phase II study. The muscle trial randomized 88 participants and found sex-dependent responses.

sections.label: Safety
sections.paragraph: Pioglitazone can cause fluid retention and can precipitate or worsen congestive heart failure, which is the subject of its boxed warning. Edema, rapid weight gain and breathlessness are therefore different from a benign change in body weight. Hypoglycemia becomes more likely when pioglitazone is combined with insulin or an insulin secretagogue, even though its principal action is improved insulin sensitivity. The label also discusses liver injury, fractures, urinary-bladder tumor concerns and macular edema as separate safety issues with different evidence and qualifications. These warnings should not be collapsed into a claim that the drug is generally safe because it is used for diabetes. Dose, treatment duration, co-medications and the patient's cardiac and other clinical characteristics all affect interpretation. A neurological, psychiatric or liver-disease repurposing study tests its own population and cannot remove the established fluid-retention and heart-failure hazards.

guide.title: Memantine
guide.description: An NMDA-receptor blocker investigated for temozolomide resistance in glioblastoma cells.

sections.label: Overview
sections.paragraph: Memantine’s glioblastoma investigation concerns NMDA signaling and temozolomide resistance. The medicine's established label context is symptomatic treatment of moderate-to-severe Alzheimer dementia through blockade of open NMDA-receptor channels. That use does not establish prevention or slowing of neurodegeneration, and it does not establish a cancer indication. The glioblastoma study tested human tumor cells, not patients, and connected NMDA signaling with MGMT, a DNA-repair protein associated with temozolomide resistance. Memantine increased temozolomide-related cell injury while reducing MGMT in that experimental setting. These are mechanistic findings with Low confidence for clinical translation. They supply neither a patient survival estimate nor a validated cancer dose, duration or tolerability profile, so the original neurological use and the tumor-cell hypothesis must remain distinct.

Conditions or medicines that alkalinize urine can reduce clearance and increase exposure. Severe kidney impairment requires a lower target dose. Combining memantine with amantadine, ketamine or dextromethorphan has not been systematically evaluated and calls for caution. The kidney and urine-pH issues both affect how much medicine remains in the body, but they are distinct from a hypersensitivity contraindication. The cited product is oral solution, whose labeled Alzheimer schedule uses gradual weekly increases and a reduced target in severe renal impairment. Those instructions provide established-use safety context rather than evidence for combining memantine with temozolomide in patients. The glioblastoma experiment used cells and supplied no clinical tolerability estimate. Its laboratory response therefore cannot establish that an effective experimental concentration can be used safely in a person, or that adding another NMDA antagonist is suitable.

sections.label: Contraindications
sections.paragraph: Hypersensitivity to memantine or a formulation ingredient is a contraindication. This is the formal restriction described for the cited product, rather than a complete account of its precautions. Severe renal impairment instead requires a lower target dose, and alkaline urine can reduce clearance and increase exposure. The label also urges caution when combining other NMDA antagonists, including amantadine, ketamine or dextromethorphan, because those combinations have not been systematically evaluated. These issues remain distinct from allergy and matter even when no hypersensitivity is present. Common adverse effects include dizziness, headache, confusion and constipation. The glioblastoma cell experiment does not establish a safe cancer regimen or resolve suitability in these clinical circumstances, because it did not administer treatment to patients or measure their tolerability.

sections.paragraph: Alkaline urine can reduce clearance. Combining other NMDA antagonists, including amantadine, ketamine, or dextromethorphan, requires caution. Reducing clearance means that the same administered amount can lead to greater exposure, making urine-pH changes relevant alongside kidney function. Severe renal impairment has its own reduced target dose in the cited oral-solution label. Combining NMDA antagonists raises a different issue from altered clearance: the label states that combinations with amantadine, ketamine and dextromethorphan have not been systematically evaluated. That caution cannot be removed by a tumor-cell experiment showing greater temozolomide-related injury. The glioblastoma report did not expose patients to a cancer regimen and provides no estimate of combination tolerability. Its mechanistic findings therefore remain separate from the clinical interaction review required when memantine is used with other medicines.
