sections.label: Dosing
sections.paragraph: Label context: The cited product is oral solution. For Alzheimer dementia, dosing begins at 5 mg daily, with increases of 5 mg separated by at least a week toward 10 mg twice daily. Severe renal impairment changes the target to 5 mg twice daily. This is approved-use context, not a glioblastoma regimen. The glioblastoma study tested cell concentrations and temozolomide combinations, not a patient schedule. The weekly interval allows the labeled schedule to be distinguished from the concentrations used in tumor-cell experiments. Severe renal impairment changes the target, and alkaline urine can reduce clearance, so the same numerical dose does not represent identical exposure in every clinical circumstance. None of those Alzheimer-label instructions establishes how much memantine would be effective or tolerable alongside temozolomide for glioblastoma. The cell study provides no patient dose-response comparison and cannot validate transferring its experimental exposure into a cancer treatment schedule.

sections.label: Evidence
sections.paragraph: MGMT biology and the cell model delimit this mechanistic evidence. The study used human glioblastoma cells to examine a link between NMDA-receptor signaling, increased MGMT expression and temozolomide resistance. Reducing MGMT alongside greater temozolomide-related cell injury is evidence about that experimental system, not a measured survival advantage. Human-derived cells do not constitute a patient treatment trial, and no clinical symptom, function or tolerability comparison was provided. Confidence in clinical translation remains Low. The separate Alzheimer label concerns symptomatic treatment and does not establish slowing of neurodegeneration or an anticancer effect. The evidence therefore supports a specific resistance-pathway hypothesis while leaving the clinical dose, treatment duration, safety and benefit for glioblastoma unestablished. A pathway change must not be substituted for those missing patient outcomes.

sections.label: Research
sections.paragraph: Translation requires determining whether NMDA blockade changes temozolomide response in patients. The existing experiment examines one proposed resistance pathway in human glioblastoma cells. NMDA signaling was linked to increased MGMT, and memantine increased temozolomide-related cell injury while reducing that DNA-repair protein. This design can connect pathway measurements within cells, but it cannot show whether patients live longer, function better or tolerate a combination. A clinical translation question therefore includes both the intended tumor effect and whether a usable exposure can be delivered safely. The cited oral-solution label supplies an Alzheimer dosing context, including renal adjustment, rather than answering that cancer question. Keeping those scopes separate preserves the mechanistic value of the cell study without describing a validated glioblastoma regimen or established clinical benefit.

guide.title: Sildenafil
guide.description: A PDE5 inhibitor with distinct pancreatic combination experiments and potentially contrary glioblastoma biology.

sections.label: Overview
sections.paragraph: Sildenafil is established for erectile dysfunction and pulmonary arterial hypertension. Its cancer investigations concern cell signaling and treatment combinations. Both established uses depend on PDE5 inhibition and smooth-muscle relaxation, but their product strengths and treatment schedules differ. The cancer rationale asks a separate question about how PDE5 blockade changes responses in particular tumor settings. Pancreatic experiments found greater cancer-cell killing during combinations with chemotherapy, while a glioblastoma cell model showed increased migration with sildenafil. A small healthy-volunteer experiment studied cerebral circulation during acute laboratory hypoxia rather than cancer treatment. These observations therefore do not supply one general anticancer or oxygenation benefit. The tumor system, treatment combination and measured endpoint determine what each report can actually support.

sections.label: Benefits
sections.paragraph: Pancreatic cell experiments found increased chemotherapy killing with PDE5 inhibitors. Glioblastoma experiments provide a counterpoint: sildenafil increased migration in one cell model. The favorable pancreatic observation concerns experimental drug combinations, including increased killing with chemotherapy agents such as gemcitabine. It does not establish that sildenafil alone controls cancer in patients. The glioblastoma finding goes in a different direction: increased migration in a cell model is an unfavorable signal, not confirmation of the pancreatic rationale. A separate experiment in healthy men measured responses to acute low oxygen. Selected vascular measures changed, but cortical oxygenation did not show a significant drug effect. These distinct observations do not demonstrate that sildenafil improves tumor oxygen delivery, neurological disease or patient cancer outcomes across clinical conditions.

sections.label: Safety
sections.paragraph: Common effects include headache, flushing, and dyspepsia. Hypotension, sudden hearing loss, and serious visual symptoms are important labeled concerns. The brief experiment enrolled healthy volunteers who were free of medication. It cannot establish safety in patients receiving chemotherapy, multiple blood-pressure medicines or long-term treatment. Its physiological observations therefore add no general clearance for those combinations and do not replace the distinct contraindications and interaction information in the prescribing labels. The pulmonary-hypertension label separately warns about pulmonary edema in patients with pulmonary veno-occlusive disease, a setting that is not interchangeable with erectile dysfunction. Rare sudden visual or hearing changes and prolonged erection require their own assessment, rather than being grouped with routine headache. These source-specific warnings explain why the indication, cardiovascular context and actual concomitant vasodilators remain important even when a study reports acceptable average tolerability.

sections.label: Contraindications
sections.paragraph: Sildenafil is contraindicated with organic nitrates, whether taken regularly or intermittently, because the combined effect can cause excessive hypotension. The pulmonary-hypertension tablet label also contraindicates concomitant riociguat, a soluble guanylate-cyclase stimulator, and use after hypersensitivity to sildenafil or a product component. These restrictions are different from precautions concerning other blood-pressure medicines, alpha blockers, particular cardiovascular conditions or altered drug exposure. The exact co-medication and its mechanism determine which category applies. The source's pulmonary vascular indication must also remain identifiable, because not every warning or dosing instruction is interchangeable with the erectile-dysfunction product. A repurposing trial's entry criteria do not replace these pharmacological restrictions, and a proposed improvement in circulation does not establish that adding another vasodilator is safe. The patient population, formulation and complete regimen remain essential to interpreting suitability.

sections.label: Interactions
sections.paragraph: Sildenafil interactions can reflect additive vasodilation or altered exposure. Nitrates and riociguat are contraindicated because their effects on vascular signaling can combine with sildenafil to lower blood pressure excessively. Alpha blockers and other antihypertensive medicines have a different set of hypotension precautions. Potent CYP3A inhibitors, including ritonavir, can increase sildenafil exposure; the cited pulmonary-hypertension label does not recommend those combinations. These product-specific instructions should not be replaced with one rule copied from another sildenafil indication or dose schedule. Medicines that lower exposure introduce a different interpretation problem from those that increase it. A study of sildenafil for a repurposed use therefore needs its actual formulation, co-medications and cardiovascular population retained. An observed physiological effect or a tolerable average response cannot establish that every additional vasodilator or metabolic inhibitor is compatible with the same regimen.

sections.label: Dosing
sections.paragraph: The pancreatic experiments used drug combinations in cell models. The PAH and erectile-dysfunction schedules are separate clinical regimens, not cancer dosing schedules. The hypoxia experiment used an initial 50 mg oral dose during normal oxygen conditions and a second 50 mg dose during the hypoxia visit, with timed measurements after administration. This describes that short laboratory protocol only. It supplies neither a cancer-treatment schedule nor evidence that repeating the protocol outside the experiment is beneficial or safe. The two 50 mg administrations belong to a short physiological experiment in healthy men, with timed measurements under different oxygen conditions. They cannot be converted into a repeated neurological or cancer-treatment schedule. The pancreatic combination work used cell models, where enhanced killing with chemotherapy is not a clinical dose-finding result. Established pulmonary arterial hypertension and erectile-dysfunction products also retain separate schedules and strengths. Their common active ingredient does not make their regimens interchangeable or provide a dose for the experimental tumor combinations. The reported protocols therefore describe what was tested without establishing a universal repurposing regimen.

sections.label: Quality
sections.paragraph: Sildenafil products used for pulmonary arterial hypertension and erectile dysfunction contain the same active molecule but have different labeled indications, strengths and schedules. The pulmonary-hypertension regimen is designed around continuing vascular treatment, while the erectile-dysfunction label has its own administration and interaction qualifications. Those differences must remain explicit when a research report names only sildenafil or quotes a milligram amount. A matching active ingredient is not enough to identify the tested intervention, and dose instructions from one labeled product cannot automatically be assigned to another indication. The actual oral preparation, administered frequency, accompanying vasodilators and drugs affecting metabolism all help determine exposure. These product distinctions also limit repurposing claims: an observed response with one schedule does not independently demonstrate equivalence or benefit for every other preparation, indication or experimental regimen sharing the sildenafil name.

sections.label: Evidence
sections.paragraph: Pancreatic support comes from experimental combination treatment. The glioblastoma report combines tumor-expression associations with mechanistic cell work, including an opposing signal. A separate randomized crossover experiment studied cerebral circulation during acute laboratory hypoxia in 12 healthy men. It found changes in selected vascular and redox measures, rather than a demonstrated improvement in cancer or neurological disease. Confidence that these physiological findings predict benefit in another clinical condition is Low: the population, short exposure and measured endpoints do not answer those treatment questions. The pancreatic cell findings and the unfavorable glioblastoma migration signal should be interpreted as different experimental responses rather than a consistent anticancer effect. The glioblastoma expression-outcome association also did not randomize patients to sildenafil. Likewise, the twelve-man hypoxia experiment tested a short physiological exposure in healthy volunteers, not treatment of a neurological disorder. Its selected vascular and redox measurements are distinct from cortical oxygenation, which did not show a significant drug effect. Clinical translation remains Low: these reports do not establish patient cancer benefit, improved tumor oxygen delivery or a long-term neurological effect from the measured laboratory changes.

guide.title: Valproic acid
guide.description: An antiseizure medicine studied as an epigenetic modifier in cancer, with important toxicity findings.

sections.label: Overview
sections.paragraph: Valproate’s oncology rationale is epigenetic, distinct from seizure control. Its combination trials make tolerability central to interpreting any response signal. Valproic acid increases inhibitory GABA activity in the brain. It also inhibits histone deacetylases, a separate action investigated in oncology. Valproate did not improve remission or survival in a randomized older-adult AML trial. A small head and neck combination trial stopped for toxicity; breast research showed histone acetylation. In the head and neck cancer trial, enrollment stopped after ten patients; nine were evaluable and the response rate was 88%, but the uncontrolled design and severe toxicity limit the benefit interpretation. The breast-cancer combination produced histone acetylation in tumor and surrogate tissues, showing pharmacologic activity. Remission was 17.8% with valproate versus 17.2% without it; odds ratio 1.06 (95% CI 0.51-2.21).

sections.label: Safety
sections.paragraph: Valproic acid carries serious warnings for liver toxicity, fetal harm and pancreatitis. The hepatic risk is particularly consequential in young children and patients with specified mitochondrial disorders, while pregnancy exposure can cause major malformations and adverse developmental outcomes. Pancreatitis can be severe and is not limited to the initial treatment period. Other important effects include thrombocytopenia or bleeding-related abnormalities, hyperammonemia, sedation and additional neurological or metabolic complications. Hyperammonemia can occur even when conventional liver tests are not abnormal, so it is a distinct clinical issue. These risks should not be reduced to a generic statement about monitoring liver enzymes. A cancer or neuropsychiatric repurposing rationale does not remove the established hazards, and trial-specific dosing, co-medications, age and reproductive context remain necessary to interpret safety. The cited source concerns a defined oral valproate product rather than every conceivable experimental exposure.

The reproductive contraindication has an indication-specific component: prophylaxis of migraine is contraindicated during pregnancy and in women of childbearing potential who are not using effective contraception. That wording must not be flattened into either an unrestricted permission for other uses or an inaccurate claim that every indication has identical regulatory language. Serious fetal risks and the source's additional benefit-risk qualifications remain important outside migraine prevention. Proposed repurposing therefore requires the actual disease, patient population and formulation to remain identifiable; study exclusions and broader precautions are not interchangeable with the formal contraindication list.

sections.label: Interactions
sections.paragraph: Valproate has clinically important interactions with other anticonvulsants and medicines from several additional classes. Enzyme-inducing drugs can increase valproate clearance, while valproate can itself alter the metabolism or protein binding of co-administered agents. Lamotrigine is an important example in which inhibited clearance changes its exposure and associated toxicity concerns. Carbapenem antibiotics can markedly reduce valproate concentrations, creating a different problem from an interaction that raises them. Topiramate is discussed in connection with hyperammonemia and encephalopathy, rather than only a concentration change. These mechanisms require separate interpretation, and changes in the accompanying regimen can matter even when the valproate dose is unchanged. A repurposing study cannot establish the safety of arbitrary anticonvulsant, psychiatric or antimicrobial combinations. The actual formulation, measured concentrations where appropriate, clinical response and co-medications must remain connected to any reported outcome.

guide.title: Parkinson disease
guide.description: Metformin’s neuroprotective rationale and the clinical results of a small Parkinson’s pilot.

sections.label: Overview
sections.paragraph: Parkinson’s disease affects movement and many nonmotor functions. Loss of dopamine-producing neurons contributes to slowness, stiffness and tremor; levodopa helps movement symptoms but does not replace lost neurons. The metformin repurposing question concerns whether adding a metabolic drug improves outcomes beyond ongoing levodopa/carbidopa. A small pilot tested that addition for three months and did not demonstrate superior clinical scores over placebo. This should remain separate from experimental investigations of autophagy, mitochondrial oxidative stress and neuronal survival in cells or mice. Changes in those proposed pathways do not establish clinical disease modification. Parkinson symptoms also extend beyond movement to sleep, mood, autonomic and cognitive function. The selected short clinical comparison therefore neither resolves all aspects of the condition nor establishes that metformin protects against long-term progression.

sections.label: Options
sections.paragraph: A metformin pilot in people already taking levodopa/carbidopa did not demonstrate better clinical scores than placebo after three months. This matters because improvement within the metformin group alone can overstate the treatment effect. Sixty participants were randomized and 52 analyzed after withdrawals in this single-center, per-protocol pilot. The post-treatment total UPDRS comparison had a P value of 0.515, and clinical subscores likewise showed no significant between-group differences. Selected biomarkers changed, including alpha-synuclein and inflammatory signaling measures, but those observations did not establish better clinical function. The intervention was an addition to existing levodopa/carbidopa over three months, rather than a replacement. Its selected population, including exclusion of diabetes and several comorbidities, also limits extension to broader Parkinson populations or a claim of long-term disease modification.

The trial studied metformin as an addition to levodopa/carbidopa, so its observations concern that treatment context rather than replacement of established Parkinson therapy. Diabetes and several comorbidities were exclusion criteria, limiting how broadly its tolerability findings can be applied. Sixty participants were randomized and 52 were included in the per-protocol analysis after withdrawals. That small, selected population and the three-month duration do not establish long-term tolerability across the wider Parkinson population. Safety must also be interpreted alongside the efficacy result: the between-group clinical comparisons did not establish superior function with the addition of metformin, despite changes in selected biomarker measures.

guide.title: Schizophrenia
guide.description: Metformin for cognitive performance and minocycline for negative symptoms: different schizophrenia research questions.

sections.label: Overview
sections.paragraph: Schizophrenia can involve psychotic symptoms, reduced motivation and expression, and cognitive difficulties such as problems with attention or working memory. These symptom domains require different outcome measures. The selected repurposing studies illustrate that distinction: metformin was added to ongoing treatment to investigate cognitive performance, whereas BeneMin tested minocycline for negative symptoms. In the 72-person open-label metformin trial, cognitive-test scores improved more than with ongoing antipsychotic treatment alone after 24 weeks. The absence of a placebo group limits interpretation. BeneMin enrolled 207 people with recent-onset illness and found no negative-symptom benefit over placebo. Those findings cannot be combined into one verdict about treating schizophrenia, because they concern different symptom domains and interventions. A later metabolic and imaging report used subsets from the metformin trial, adding exploratory biological observations rather than an independent clinical replication.

The metformin study randomized 72 people, was open-label and had no placebo group; at 24 weeks its between-group MCCB composite-score difference was 3.43 points, with a 95% confidence interval from 1.83 to 5.02. BeneMin enrolled 207 people with recent-onset schizophrenia and compared minocycline with placebo as an addition to ongoing treatment. Its negative-symptom difference was -0.19 points, with an interval from -1.23 to 0.85, indicating no demonstrated advantage on that endpoint. Cognitive performance and negative symptoms are different treatment targets, so these results do not rank metformin above minocycline for the same clinical purpose. The exploratory metabolic companion analysis also remains part of the original metformin trial rather than a second confirmation of benefit.

sections.label: Overview
sections.paragraph: Alzheimer’s disease disrupts communication between neurons, damages their connections and ultimately causes cell death. Inflammation involving brain immune cells is one process investigated as a treatment target. This disease process extends beyond normal age-related changes in thinking because neuronal connections and brain function become widely damaged. Repurposing studies have asked whether medicines with anti-inflammatory rationales can alter cognitive decline or everyday functioning. The two-year MADE minocycline trial found neither cognitive nor functional benefit in mild Alzheimer's disease, despite that rationale. A separate small thalidomide trial in mild-to-moderate disease also found no cognitive benefit and had poor tolerability. These are patient-outcome questions rather than evidence that reducing an inflammatory signal necessarily changes the course of illness. The population, duration and ability to continue treatment all matter when interpreting whether an experimental approach affects meaningful disease outcomes.

sections.label: Options
sections.paragraph: In the two-year MADE trial, minocycline did not slow cognitive or functional decline in people with mild Alzheimer’s disease. The higher tested dose was also poorly tolerated. MADE included 544 eligible participants at 32 memory clinics and tested 200 or 400 mg daily against placebo. The combined minocycline groups differed from placebo by about 0.1 points on the standardized Mini-Mental State Examination, with a 95% confidence interval from -1.1 to 1.2. Daily-function ratings likewise failed to show benefit. The separate thalidomide phase IIa trial involved 25 people with mild-to-moderate disease over 24 weeks; 14 terminated early and the target dose was not sustained. That study did not establish cognitive benefit either. These findings retain the difference between a proposed anti-inflammatory mechanism and an intervention that actually improves cognition, function or disease progression.

sections.label: Safety
sections.paragraph: Gastrointestinal symptoms, dizziness and skin effects contributed to treatment discontinuation, especially in the higher-dose group. MADE tested 200 and 400 mg daily over two years, and the higher-dose regimen was poorly tolerated. The consequences include the ability to remain on treatment, not simply whether a symptom appears on an adverse-event list. Lower follow-up in the high-dose arm is also relevant when interpreting the clinical results. Another anti-inflammatory repurposing study, the small thalidomide trial, had 14 of 25 participants terminate early and did not sustain its target dose. That is a separate drug and cannot define minocycline's adverse-effect rate, but it illustrates why tolerability remains part of evaluating these actual regimens. Neither study demonstrated cognitive benefit that would establish a favorable treatment balance for Alzheimer's disease.

sections.label: Comparisons
sections.paragraph: Two minocycline doses were compared with placebo. Neither established disease modification over two years; the result concerns symptomatic mild Alzheimer’s disease. The minocycline study measured both cognition and daily function, so a proposed inflammatory mechanism cannot replace the negative patient-outcome comparisons. Its combined cognitive estimate was about 0.1 standardized Mini-Mental State Examination points different from placebo, with uncertainty spanning -1.1 to 1.2. Thalidomide was tested separately in a much smaller, 24-week study of mild-to-moderate disease and was poorly tolerated, with no demonstrated cognitive benefit. These are not head-to-head data between the two medicines. Different disease severity, treatment duration and treatment continuation limit cross-trial rankings. The relevant conclusion is that neither cited approach established benefit in its own studied population, rather than that the trials identify one anti-inflammatory drug as superior to the other.

sections.label: Evidence
sections.paragraph: MADE included 544 eligible participants at 32 memory clinics. Cognitive testing and daily-function ratings both failed to show benefit, strengthening the negative clinical conclusion. The study randomized 554 people, with 544 eligible for analysis, and the higher-dose arm had poorer tolerability and lower follow-up. The near-zero combined cognitive difference and the lack of functional improvement address the intended clinical benefit, rather than simply a biological pathway. The separate thalidomide trial was much smaller: 25 participants, 24 weeks of follow-up and 14 early terminations, with a target dose that was not sustained. It found no cognitive benefit but has important attrition and exposure limitations. These studies should remain separate rather than adding unlike participants into a single efficacy estimate. Together they show why laboratory anti-inflammatory reasoning cannot substitute for actual cognitive and daily-function findings.

guide.title: Multiple sclerosis
guide.description: Minocycline after a first demyelinating episode, with separate six-month and two-year results.

sections.label: Overview
sections.paragraph: Multiple sclerosis damages myelin and nerve fibers in the central nervous system. A clinically isolated syndrome is a first neurological episode suggestive of inflammatory demyelination; it is a specific early setting for treatment research. The selected minocycline trial studied that first-episode setting, rather than every form or stage of multiple sclerosis. Its anti-inflammatory and neuroprotective rationale goes beyond the drug's antibiotic use. At six months, fewer participants met conversion criteria with minocycline than placebo, but the difference was not statistically significant at the two-year secondary timepoint. More rash, dizziness, dental discoloration and withdrawals also occurred with active treatment. The early result therefore needs both its timing and tolerability context. It does not establish an effect on progressive disease, long-term disability or superiority to a licensed disease-modifying MS therapy.

sections.label: Options
sections.paragraph: Minocycline reduced conversion to multiple sclerosis over six months in a trial after a first demyelinating episode. The difference was not statistically significant at the two-year secondary timepoint. The trial enrolled 142 participants after a first demyelinating episode. Adjusting for baseline enhancing MRI lesions, the six-month risk difference was 18.5 percentage points in favor of minocycline, with a 95% confidence interval from 3.7 to 33.3 points. That early conversion result is the supported finding. It should not be extended to progressive MS, long-term disability prevention or superiority over licensed therapy, because the comparison used placebo in a specific early setting. Rash, dizziness, dental discoloration and withdrawals were also more frequent with minocycline. The later nonsignificant conversion result remains part of interpreting the durability of this experimental approach.

A separate computational drug-matching analysis supplies no treated-patient comparison and should not be used to strengthen the minocycline clinical estimate.

guide.title: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis
guide.description: Minocycline in ALS: harmful functional trial results, uncertain mortality findings and the limits of a laboratory neuroprotection rationale.

sections.label: Overview
sections.paragraph: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis damages the motor neurons that control voluntary muscles. Progressive weakness can affect movement, speech, swallowing and breathing, making physical function and support needs central to evaluating an intervention. Minocycline was investigated because of neuroprotective laboratory findings, but the selected randomized trial produced a harmful rather than beneficial functional result. Among 412 participants followed during nine months of the tested regimen, functional scores declined faster than with placebo. That finding should remain separate from the uncertain mortality comparison and from individual adverse-event risks. A medicine can fail its hoped-for neuroprotective role on a directly measured functional endpoint even when the study cannot prove a difference in survival. For ALS, experimental pathway reasoning therefore needs to be evaluated against movement and daily-function outcomes rather than treated as evidence of preserved motor neurons in patients.

sections.label: Options
sections.paragraph: Clinical evidence is Moderate for harmful functional decline with the tested minocycline regimen. In the randomized 412-person ALS trial, ALSFRS-R scores declined by 1.30 points per month with minocycline and 1.04 points per month with placebo over nine months. The difference was statistically significant, with P=0.005, and contradicted the hoped-for neuroprotective benefit in that setting. This is a condition-specific clinical finding, not proof that minocycline has the same effect in every neurological disease or at every regimen. Mortality was numerically higher but uncertain and not statistically significant, so it must not inherit the primary functional outcome's assessment. Non-serious gastrointestinal and neurological events were also more common, without establishing that they caused the faster decline. These separate results support a clear unfavorable functional conclusion while preserving uncertainty about other outcomes.

guide.title: Vitiligo
guide.description: Atorvastatin’s immune rationale and its unsuccessful addition to narrowband UV-B for active vitiligo.

sections.label: Overview
sections.paragraph: Vitiligo causes loss of pigment when melanocytes are destroyed or stop functioning. Autoimmune processes are important in the disease, and visible skin changes can substantially affect quality of life. Repurposing research asks whether changing immune or inflammatory processes can influence disease activity or repigmentation. The atorvastatin trial discussed here selected active nonsegmental vitiligo and added the medicine to narrowband UV-B phototherapy. Both treatment groups improved, but the comparison did not establish extra benefit from atorvastatin. This distinction matters because improvement during combined treatment does not show which part of the regimen produced it. Disease extent, spreading and effects on quality of life are also distinct outcomes, and a change in one does not automatically demonstrate benefit across all of them.

sections.label: Options
sections.paragraph: A small randomized trial did not find that adding atorvastatin improved the effect of narrowband UV-B phototherapy on active nonsegmental vitiligo. The trial randomized 30 people and analyzed 29 over six months. Scores improved in both treatment groups, but the between-group VASI comparison was not significant, with P=0.49. Improvement while receiving atorvastatin plus phototherapy therefore cannot be assigned to atorvastatin rather than the shared phototherapy or other influences. The study assessed both vitiligo area and spreading, without demonstrating a significant added effect. Its small sample also limits precision, so lack of significance should not be presented as proof that the two regimens are exactly equivalent. The clinically supported finding is narrower: this particular add-on study did not establish extra benefit for its selected active nonsegmental-vitiligo population and treatment period.

sections.label: Safety
sections.paragraph: Ten participants receiving atorvastatin reported adverse events, including muscle pain and gastrointestinal symptoms. One developed a transient muscle-enzyme elevation that resolved after dose reduction. These observations occurred while atorvastatin was added to narrowband UV-B phototherapy in a small study of active nonsegmental vitiligo. They describe tolerability of that combination rather than a guarantee about atorvastatin alone or every vitiligo regimen. Muscle symptoms and the enzyme elevation are distinct observations, and resolution after a dose reduction does not establish that similar effects cannot recur. The trial randomized only 30 people, so it cannot precisely characterize uncommon harms or longer-term safety. Those limitations matter alongside the finding of no significant added vitiligo benefit. An improvement seen in both groups should not be assigned to atorvastatin as an offsetting benefit when the direct comparison did not establish one.

sections.label: Comparisons
sections.paragraph: The direct comparison was atorvastatin plus phototherapy versus the same phototherapy alone over six months. It did not establish extra benefit from atorvastatin. Using the same phototherapy in both groups allowed the study to ask about atorvastatin's incremental contribution. Both groups improved, which is different from demonstrating that the added medicine caused improvement. The VASI between-group comparison had P=0.49, and measures of spreading also failed to show a significant added effect. Because 30 people were randomized and 29 analyzed, uncertainty remains substantial and the negative result does not prove exact equivalence. It also cannot rank atorvastatin against unrelated vitiligo treatments that were not included. The conclusion should retain the active nonsegmental population, six-month period and shared narrowband UV-B background treatment, rather than generalizing a treatment change during follow-up into an atorvastatin-specific benefit.

guide.title: Sarcopenia
guide.description: Metformin studies of walking speed and muscle adaptation in older adults.

sections.label: Overview
sections.paragraph: Sarcopenia involves declining muscle strength and function, often with reduced muscle mass. Difficulty rising from a chair, slower walking and increased falls can threaten independence. Resistance activity and adequate nutrition are central to preserving muscle health. This makes the endpoint important when evaluating a repurposed medicine: walking performance, strength and muscle size are related but different measures. MET-PREVENT tested metformin in 72 older adults with prefrailty or frailty and found no detectable walking-speed advantage over four months. MASTERS instead examined adaptation during progressive resistance training and found smaller muscle-size gains with metformin; differences in strength gains were not significant. These studies challenge a general assumption that improving metabolism necessarily improves muscle aging. Their selected populations and interventions should remain distinct, with physical function assessed directly rather than inferred solely from a change in muscle mass.

sections.paragraph: Metformin did not improve walking speed in MET-PREVENT. A separate resistance-training trial found smaller gains in muscle size with metformin, challenging the idea that a diabetes drug necessarily improves muscle aging. In MET-PREVENT, 72 older adults with prefrailty or frailty had a four-month between-group walking-speed difference of 0.001 m/s, with a 95% confidence interval from -0.06 to 0.06. That estimate is compatible with a small decline or a small improvement and does not demonstrate better mobility. MASTERS addresses a different intervention context, progressive resistance training, where metformin blunted muscle-size gains. Strength-gain differences were not statistically significant, so the size finding should not be described as proven impairment of strength. These results retain separate populations and endpoints rather than establishing one uniform effect on sarcopenia.

sections.label: Safety
sections.paragraph: Metformin was poorly tolerated in MET-PREVENT, a four-month trial in older adults with prefrailty or frailty and impaired physical function. Renal function, gastrointestinal symptoms and vitamin B12 are also relevant to longer-term metformin exposure in this population. These safety considerations should be read alongside the absence of a detectable walking-speed benefit, rather than treating the drug's established metabolic role as evidence of improved mobility. MASTERS addresses a different concern during progressive resistance training: metformin blunted gains in muscle size, while differences in strength gains were not statistically significant. That finding is a training-adaptation result rather than an estimate of the same adverse events measured in MET-PREVENT. The two studies should retain their separate populations, treatment contexts and outcomes.

sections.label: Comparisons
sections.paragraph: Walking speed, strength and muscle mass are different outcomes. MET-PREVENT and MASTERS studied different populations and interventions, so their results should be understood separately. MET-PREVENT examined a four-month walking-speed outcome in 72 older adults with prefrailty or frailty, finding a difference of 0.001 m/s and a confidence interval spanning small changes in either direction. MASTERS tested the response to progressive resistance training and found blunted muscle-size gains with metformin, without statistically significant strength-gain differences. One trial therefore addresses mobility in an impaired older population, while the other addresses adaptation to a structured training intervention. They provide complementary evidence rather than independent repetitions of the same endpoint. Combining them into one favorable muscle-aging claim would conceal both the negative walking result and the less favorable size response.

guide.title: Vorinostat
guide.description: An HDAC inhibitor nominated for anti-TNF-refractory Crohn’s disease through gene-expression analysis.

sections.label: Overview
sections.paragraph: Vorinostat is a cancer medicine with an epigenetic mechanism. Its Crohn’s connection arises from an analysis of anti-TNF-refractory disease transcriptomes. The labeled medicine inhibits several histone deacetylases, changing protein acetylation and gene regulation; its specified indication is cutaneous T-cell lymphoma. The Crohn's analysis instead compared existing disease gene-expression patterns with compound signatures. It nominated vorinostat for a chemokine- and cytokine-related molecular cluster but did not administer the drug or measure remission. The result has Low confidence for clinical translation, because a computational match does not establish an intestinal treatment effect or tolerability. The underlying patient dataset should not be counted as a drug-exposed cohort. Its cancer-label dosing, safety monitoring and formulation instructions remain established-use context rather than a validated course for anti-TNF-refractory Crohn's disease.

sections.label: Benefits
sections.paragraph: Clinical evidence: Low for Crohn's disease. Vorinostat emerged from a computational analysis of anti-TNF-refractory disease transcriptomes. The study did not administer vorinostat or measure remission, symptom improvement or gastrointestinal tolerability. Its established cancer indication supplies clinical context, but cannot establish benefit for Crohn's disease. The analysis used GSE100833 and compound-signature matching to identify a hypothesis for experimental testing. Its vorinostat enrichment score of 12.3 refers to one selected molecular cluster, not a remission percentage or probability that a patient will improve. The source describes transcriptomes from 327 patients, but those people were not a newly treated vorinostat cohort. Reliance on one dataset, possible selection bias and the need for confirmation limit how broadly the nomination applies. Clinical translation therefore remains Low, with no treated-patient comparison, clinical effect interval or evidence that vorinostat safely controls intestinal inflammation after anti-TNF treatment has failed.

sections.label: Safety
sections.paragraph: Label context: Thrombocytopenia, anemia, thromboembolism, hyperglycemia and dehydration are important risks. Blood counts, glucose, electrolytes and kidney-related chemistry need scheduled monitoring. Low potassium or magnesium should be corrected before treatment. Other HDAC inhibitors, including valproic acid, can add severe thrombocytopenia and gastrointestinal bleeding concerns; warfarin requires INR monitoring. These are cancer-label risks and monitoring requirements, not adverse-event rates established in a Crohn's treatment trial. The transcriptomic analysis did not administer vorinostat and therefore cannot resolve gastrointestinal tolerability or determine whether a nominated molecular pattern identifies a safer subgroup. Pregnancy can involve fetal harm, and hepatic impairment can require dose reduction. The label lists no formal contraindications, but that does not remove these precautions or the need to interpret blood counts and chemistry during treatment. A favorable computational score supplies no evidence that the risks are smaller in refractory Crohn's disease than in the product's established treatment context.

sections.label: Interactions
sections.paragraph: Warfarin can show increased INR. Other HDAC inhibitors, including valproic acid, have been associated with severe thrombocytopenia and gastrointestinal bleeding. Warfarin-related INR changes concern anticoagulant effect, while combining another HDAC inhibitor raises distinct platelet and bleeding concerns. The two mechanisms therefore call for separate interpretation rather than one general statement that a combination is tolerated. Vorinostat's own label also identifies thrombocytopenia and anemia and requires blood-count monitoring, making the platelet issue relevant to its underlying safety profile. Scheduled glucose, electrolyte and kidney-related chemistry monitoring addresses additional risks, including hyperglycemia and dehydration. These precautions belong to the established product context. The Crohn's analysis neither administered vorinostat nor tested interacting combinations, so its compound score cannot validate coadministration or establish gastrointestinal safety in patients whose disease is refractory to anti-TNF treatment.

guide.title: Thalidomide
guide.description: An established myeloma medicine whose other repurposing trials show disease-specific benefits, limitations, and harms.

sections.label: Overview
sections.paragraph: Thalidomide’s clinical results differ markedly between myeloma, ovarian cancer, and Alzheimer’s disease. Thalidomide binds cereblon, part of an E3 ubiquitin-ligase complex. It alters immune signaling and angiogenesis; its effects include context-dependent changes in TNF-alpha. Thalidomide-dexamethasone improves myeloma control. The ovarian comparison favored tamoxifen for safety, and the Alzheimer’s trial showed no cognitive benefit. Thalidomide did not reduce progression relative to tamoxifen and was associated with higher mortality: hazard ratio 1.76 (95% CI 1.16-2.68). PSA declines greater than 50% occurred in 53% with docetaxel-thalidomide versus 37% with docetaxel alone; progression-free survival was not significantly different (p=0.32). Adding thalidomide to irinotecan, fluorouracil, and leucovorin did not significantly improve response or time to progression. Myeloma labeling includes randomized efficacy studies; ovarian evidence is phase III; the small Alzheimer’s trial suffered high attrition.

sections.label: Safety
sections.paragraph: Thalidomide can cause severe fetal harm, including major birth defects after very limited exposure, and its U.S. distribution is restricted through a risk-management program. This risk is distinct from its other major hazards. Venous thromboembolism is particularly important in multiple-myeloma combinations, while peripheral neuropathy can be persistent or irreversible. Somnolence, constipation, dizziness, bradycardia and blood-cell abnormalities introduce additional monitoring and tolerability concerns. The accompanying regimen affects the overall risk, so safety information from one disease or combination should not become a single drug-wide rate. Pregnancy prevention, neurological assessment and thrombosis risk therefore address different clinical questions. A proposed anti-inflammatory or anticancer benefit does not remove any of these hazards. The exact indication, co-medications, dose, treatment duration and patient population remain essential when comparing labeled use with a repurposing study.

Pregnancy is not simply one caution among many: the source describes a powerful human teratogenic effect and severe, life-threatening birth defects even after a single dose. The restricted U.S. distribution program imposes pregnancy-prevention, testing and other requirements on eligible patients and healthcare participants. Those program conditions are separate from the warnings about thrombosis, neuropathy, sedation and blood-cell abnormalities. A person outside the formal contraindication categories still requires assessment of those substantial risks and the actual treatment regimen. The distinctions are especially important in combinations for multiple myeloma or other investigated conditions, where co-treatments can change toxicity. A study's inclusion rules do not replace the regulatory requirements, and a proposed repurposing use does not create an exception to the pregnancy prohibition or product hypersensitivity restriction.

guide.title: Aging & longevity
guide.description: What drug studies tell us about lifespan, physical function and other outcomes of aging.
guide.scope: Human health and function in later life, alongside the animal experiments motivating longevity research.

sections.label: Overview
sections.paragraph: Healthy aging includes maintaining physical, mental and cognitive function, independence and quality of life. Longevity research also asks whether interventions can extend lifespan; these are related but distinct goals. The selected human trials address narrower questions within healthy aging. PEARL studied body composition over 48 weeks in generally healthy adults aged 50-85; its primary visceral-adiposity result was not significant. MET-PREVENT instead studied walking speed over four months in older adults with impaired physical function and found no detectable advantage with metformin. Rapamycin's mouse lifespan experiments do directly measure survival, but they remain animal evidence. These distinctions make maintaining function and extending life separate evidentiary questions. A secondary body-composition change in a small human subgroup cannot establish longer life or define a general anti-aging treatment benefit.

sections.label: Options
sections.paragraph: Rapamycin has extended survival in mice, while the selected human studies address shorter-term outcomes. PEARL tested compounded rapamycin in generally healthy adults aged 50 to 85 and did not demonstrate improvement in its primary visceral-adiposity outcome. A secondary finding of increased lean tissue in women receiving the higher study dose came from a small subgroup amid multiple comparisons. It does not establish longer life or improved physical function, and the completer analysis excluded eleven dropouts. MET-PREVENT instead evaluated walking speed in older adults with impaired function and found no detectable metformin advantage. MASTERS found smaller lean-mass gains with metformin during resistance training. These different populations and endpoints do not establish one broadly beneficial longevity regimen or show that a favorable animal survival result translates into longer human life.

sections.label: Evidence
sections.paragraph: PEARL randomized 125 people and analyzed 114 completers over 48 weeks. Its primary visceral-adiposity outcome was not significantly different from placebo; dose-specific confidence intervals included no difference. A secondary lean-tissue finding in women at the higher study dose has uncertain clinical importance because the subgroup was small, multiple comparisons were performed and missing outcomes were excluded. The compounded product also produced lower measured exposure than commercial sirolimus, and all authors reported employment or ownership interests in AgelessRx. These limitations accompany the findings rather than proving that the observation is false. The mouse experiments directly measured survival, whereas MET-PREVENT measured four-month walking performance without a detectable metformin benefit. Different species, populations, endpoints and durations prevent those records from becoming one demonstration of human lifespan extension.

sections.label: Safety
sections.paragraph: Sirolimus can increase infection risk, impair wound healing and raise blood lipids. Strong CYP3A and P-glycoprotein interactions, including grapefruit, can alter exposure. Metformin has a different safety profile: gastrointestinal effects and vitamin B12 depletion are relevant, while severe kidney impairment increases the risk of lactic acidosis. These established product risks remain distinct from whether either drug improves a particular aging outcome. PEARL studied generally healthy adults aged 50-85, whereas MET-PREVENT enrolled much older adults with impaired physical function and reported poor metformin tolerability. The different populations do not establish one universal benefit and harm balance for aging. PEARL also used compounded rapamycin with substantially lower measured blood concentrations than commercial formulations, so its nominal doses cannot be assumed equivalent to commercial tablets.

sections.label: Comparisons
sections.paragraph: PEARL studied generally healthy adults aged 50-85, whereas MET-PREVENT recruited much older adults with impaired physical function. The different populations and outcomes do not support ranking these drugs for a single “anti-aging” benefit. PEARL analyzed 114 completers after 48 weeks and excluded eleven dropouts, with a nonsignificant primary visceral-adiposity result. MET-PREVENT examined a four-month walking-speed comparison in older adults with prefrailty or frailty and found no detectable benefit. Those are different questions from rapamycin's direct mouse survival experiments. Even the human rapamycin exposure requires care: PEARL used compounded material with substantially lower measured blood concentrations than commercial formulations. A nominal weekly dose cannot therefore define an equivalent commercial regimen. The existing studies do not directly compare these drugs for human lifespan, nor do their different endpoints provide a common scale for ranking longevity benefit.
